# Capability index

<!-- @ref LLP 0061#2-the-capability-index-registry-lite-with-witnesses — witnesses, GAP rows, and the joined surfaces -->

Every author-facing capability Snapback has, whether or not the guide
covers it yet. **GAP** rows are capabilities with no page — explicit, owned,
and dated, never silent. Shipped rows carry a code **witness** proving the
capability exists. The surface map below classifies every entry of the two
machine-enumerable registries (server routes, host-ops); `scripts/check-guide.mjs`
joins it against the code on every run, so a shipped surface cannot fall out
of this file unnoticed.

Guide owner: `ccheever`. File gaps as Linear issues in the Exact project
with the Snapback label and `guide-gap` in the title.

<img src="../brand/snapback-mark.svg" alt="Snapback" width="96" />

# The Snapback Guide

How to build an application **on** Snapback — a complete backend that
scales to zero and back up: schema and functions, server-authoritative
data, live queries, ephemeral realtime, auth, and the client arms — taught
intent-first, with code that ran in CI.

**Audience:** agents (primarily) and humans (secondarily) building on
Snapback. In a checkout, read this corpus directly. Outside a checkout, a
running Snapback server exposes the same build-bound corpus at
`GET /_snapback/guide`, individual paths below that prefix, and the complete
single-request projection at `GET /_snapback/guide/flat.md`. Those responses
carry `x-snapback-guide-content-sha256` and
`x-snapback-server-build-commit`, so a consumer can refuse to combine cached
guide bytes with a different server build. Building Snapback itself is a
different job — that's `AGENTS.md` and the LLP corpus, not this guide.

For MCP clients, run `snapback mcp`. The read-only server exposes the same
manifest, flat projection, and manifest-named pages at stable
`snapback-guide://` resource URIs. Every resource repeats the guide content
hash and build commit in MCP metadata; read the manifest first and refuse to
combine resources whose identities differ. This resource-only command exposes
no mutation or host-operation tools.

**Start every task here:** check the
[capability index](./capabilities.md) first — it lists everything Snapback
has, including what this guide doesn't cover yet (explicit GAP rows), so
you never build around a feature because you didn't know it existed.

## The map

### Getting started
- [Your first backend](./getting-started/your-first-backend.md) — schema,
  functions, handlers, seed, codegen, load, query.
- [The authoring loop](./getting-started/the-authoring-loop.md) — edit →
  regenerate → acceptance test → inspect, including the packaged
  `new`/`generate`/`dev`/`doctor` loop.

### Backend
- [Queries](./backend/queries.md) — indexed snapshot reads, server scoping,
  and the ordinary-vs-live boundary.
- [Mutations](./backend/mutations.md) — buffered writes, one commit version,
  read-set conflict validation, and structured results.
- [Safe standard patterns](./backend/standard-patterns.md) — owner-scoped CRUD,
  unique lookup, keyset pages, and server-derived time and IDs.
- [Relational queries](./backend/relational-queries.md) — bounded two-source
  equi-joins with explicit visibility and closed projections (experimental).
- [Actions and outbound fetch](./backend/actions-and-fetch.md) — gated
  egress, config grants, and mutation-owned durable effects.
- [Streamed actions](./backend/streamed-actions.md) — bounded pull-driven
  response streaming, the attempt control plane, and durable progress.
- [Scheduled execution](./backend/cron.md) — action-backed jobs,
  demand activation, deterministic ticks, and the run ledger.

### Realtime
- [Live queries](./realtime/live-queries.md) — subscriptions, snapshot +
  replace/delta, durable push, the connection axis.
- [Ephemeral state](./realtime/ephemeral-state.md) — typed rooms, all
  collection options and key modes, overlays, recovery, and Contract links.

### Sync and offline
- [Offline retention and mutation replay](./sync/offline-and-retention.md) —
  stale boot, durable outbox ordering, deterministic overlays, and settlement.

### Auth
- [Sessions and principals](./auth/sessions-and-principals.md) — the server
  derives who you are; scoped queries; logout barriers.
- [Protecting live and retained data](./auth/protecting-data.md) —
  connection grants, invalidation obligations, recovery, and authorized leases.
- [Scoped roles and memberships](./auth/scoped-roles.md) — declare app-wide or
  per-resource roles; gate queries; check and change membership safely.
- [Agent principals](./auth/agent-principals.md) — register, pair, mint scoped
  tokens, fence custody, revoke, and verify an agent journey.
- [Targets — what each one claims](./auth/targets.md) — local vs hosted
  honesty; how to check the server instead of trusting prose.

### Clients
- [The headless client](./clients/headless.md) — the complete
  `SnapbackClient` surface: calls, live/ephemeral state, receipts, and auth.
- [The app CLI](./clients/app-cli.md) — discover generated operations and run
  the packaged local agent journey without source-diving.
- [The Contract adapter](./clients/contract-adapter.md) — generated
  bindings, one-surface boot, derived optimistic overlays, offline classes.
- [The React client](./clients/react.md) — first-class external-store hook,
  keyed sibling sharing, Strict Mode lifecycle, and settlement state.
- [React Expo Online clients](./clients/react-expo.md) — the shared React
  projection on native carriers, per-OS evidence, and Online/Parity honesty.

### Testing
- [Acceptance testing](./testing/acceptance.md) — headless-first harness,
  vacuous-pass protection, safe server lifecycle.

### Operating
- [Secrets and deployment config](./operating/secrets-and-config.md) —
  declare, set, verify, grant, and consume write-only values.
- [Host operations](./operating/host-ops.md) — the complete CLI/HTTP
  operation inventory and its authority envelopes.
- [Diagnostics](./operating/diagnostics.md) — stable codes, assertion
  discipline, doctor, and bootstrap failure vocabulary.
- [Admin console](./operating/admin-console.md) — build, launch, develop, and
  debug through the privileged Contract system app.

### Deploying
- [Cloudflare proof](./deploying/cloudflare.md) — deploy and verify All
  Aboard on the honest partial hosted profile; explicit supported subset and gaps.

### Recipes
- [Presence cursors](./recipes/presence-cursors.md) — ephemeral rooms, TTL,
  publish budgets (the cursors-web demo, distilled).
- [Hidden hands](./recipes/hidden-hands.md) — per-principal secrecy, logout
  blanking, lease-bounded offline retention (card-game, distilled).

### Meta
- [Capability index](./capabilities.md) — everything Snapback has, covered
  or GAP.
- [Conventions](./conventions.md) — page rules, snippet classes, link
  policy, freshness.
- [Retrieval eval protocol](./retrieval-eval.md) — how we verify a cold
  agent actually finds these pages.

## How to trust the code here

Every `js`/`ts`/`contract` snippet marked `source=` is a verbatim excerpt
of a file CI executes end-to-end — `scripts/check-guide.mjs` fails the
build if a snippet drifts from its source. Prose can rot; these can't
silently. Pages carry `targets:` and `maturity:` frontmatter so a claim's
scope is always explicit ([conventions](./conventions.md)).

The deeper design rationale lives in the LLP corpus (`llp/`) — every page's
`authorities:` frontmatter names its sources. The demos (`demos/`) are the
full working applications these pages distill.

# Guide conventions

<!-- @ref LLP 0061#design — the corpus rules this file operationalizes -->

These are the rules every page under `guide/` follows. They are adapted from
the Exact guide's conventions (Exact LLP 0365 §1) as a **compatible core plus
Snapback extensions**, so an agent that has used either guide can navigate
the other. `scripts/check-guide.mjs` enforces the mechanical parts.

## Frontmatter

Every `.md` file under `guide/` opens with YAML frontmatter using the **flat
subset only**: `key: value` scalars and inline arrays (`key: [a, b]`). No
nested maps, no block sequences — the checker parses exactly this subset.

Fields (schema: [`frontmatter.schema.json`](./frontmatter.schema.json)):

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `title` | yes | Human title. |
| `id` | yes | Stable dotted id (`clients.contract-adapter`). Used by nav, links, the capability index, and reserved as the resource id for later projections (MCP, console). Never renamed casually. |
| `order` | yes | Deterministic ordering within the section. |
| `audience` | yes | `agent-first`. |
| `capabilities` | yes | Capability-index ids this page claims coverage of (`[]` for meta pages). |
| `authorities` | yes | Repo paths (LLPs and code) this page derives from. Freshness compares these against `reviewed-commit`. |
| `examples` | yes | Demo directories/files that exercise what the page teaches (`[]` if none). |
| `status` | yes | `draft` \| `current` \| `deprecated` — authored lifecycle. |
| `targets` | yes | `[local]`, `[local, cloudflare]`, or `[all]` for genuinely target-independent material. Local-only pages render a banner line (see below). |
| `maturity` | yes | `shipped` \| `partial` \| `design-only`, consistent with the capability index. |
| `reviewed` | yes | Date of the last intentional review — display metadata only. |
| `reviewed-commit` | yes | The commit the page was last reviewed at — the freshness **identity**. Bumping it is a deliberate act in a review pass; no tool regenerates it. `HEAD` is permitted only in the same change that creates or fully revises the page. |

`targets:` and `maturity:` are the honesty boundary made mechanical
(LLP 0060's posture): a page must never generalize a local-target guarantee
into a hosted claim. A `maturity: partial` page names what works and what
doesn't. `design-only` material may appear only inside an explicitly marked
**Design reference** section, never as a technique. Auth pages teach only
behavior witnessed by an acceptance test or the server's own
capability/inspect reporting.

### Banner

Pages with `targets: [local]` start the body with:

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](./auth/targets.md).

## Headings

Intent-first: name sections for what the reader wants to do ("Subscribe to a
query", "Scope a query to the signed-in user"), not for internal subsystem
names, so grep-by-goal works. Where a page covers an enumerable surface, it
lists **all** of it — sampling is how capabilities go undiscovered. Each
teaching page ends with an **Anti-patterns** section naming what not to
hand-roll.

## Links

Two classes, checked:

- **Corpus-internal links** are relative paths within `guide/`
  (`../realtime/live-queries.md`). They must resolve.
- **Out-of-corpus references** — `authorities:`, `examples:`, and inline
  bridges into `llp/`, `demos/`, `src/`, etc. — use repo-root paths in
  frontmatter and the `repo:` scheme inline
  (`[LLP 0008](repo:llp/0008-local-first-sync-and-realtime.rfc.md)`). They
  must exist in the repo.
- **Cross-repository references** use the shared
  `repo(<repository>):<repo-root-relative-path>` form, for example
  `[the Exact guide](repo(exact):guide/index.md)`. The repository token is
  lowercase ASCII (`[a-z0-9._-]+`); the path is relative, contains no `..`,
  and may carry a heading anchor. When a sibling checkout is present the
  checker verifies the path; without one it degrades honestly rather than
  claiming the remote bytes were checked. Exact uses the same convention and
  points its `data.snapback` external-authority row back to this guide.

## Code snippets

Every fenced `js` / `mjs` / `ts` / `tsx` / `json` / `contract` block carries
a declared class in its info string; the checker fails on unclassified
fences in those languages.

- **Transcluded-verified (the default):**
  <code>```js source=demos/todo/tests/acceptance/headless.mjs</code>
  The fence body must be an exact contiguous excerpt of the named file
  (leading indentation may be uniformly stripped; trailing whitespace is
  normalized). The named file must be exercised by CI — a demo acceptance
  suite, package test, or proof script. Drift in the source breaks the
  check, which is the point: the snippet's "this ran" property is inherited
  from CI, and behavioral drift becomes structural breakage. Update the page
  in the same change that changes the source.
- **Fragment:** <code>```js fragment reason="mid-file excerpt"</code>
  Not verified; the reason is mandatory so partial code is a tracked class,
  not an escape hatch.
- **Standalone-runnable:** reserved (LLP 0061 §Design 3). The scratch-app
  assembler is built only when a technique no CI-exercised file demonstrates
  needs a snippet; until then the checker rejects the class with a pointer
  to this paragraph. Prefer adding the technique to a demo or fixture and
  transcluding it.

`sh` fences are illustrative commands and exempt from mechanical
verification; keep them real and current. `text`, `yaml`, and diagram fences
are exempt.

**Exact-dependent snippets** (Contract-arm sources): the text match runs
everywhere with no Exact dependency. The *execution* guarantee is inherited
from the suite that runs the source file — Contract-arm suites are gated by
`SNAPBACK_VERIFY_EXACT`, which merge/release CI pins to `1`, so those
sources are always executed before landing even when a local core-only run
skipped them. The manifest records each snippet's source so a consumer can
see which suite carries its guarantee.

## The capability index

[`capabilities.md`](./capabilities.md) is authored, not generated. Shipped
rows carry a **witness** — a route in the declared registry, a host-op id, a
package export, a generated-manifest field, or a CLI command proving the
capability exists in code. Uncovered capabilities are explicit **GAP** rows
naming an owner and a review date. The checker joins the index's surface map
against the repo's declared enumerations (route registry, host-ops) — every
enumerated entry maps to a capability id or a `notAuthorFacing`
classification.

## The manifest

[`guide-manifest.generated.json`](./guide-manifest.generated.json) is
generated by `scripts/generate-guide-manifest.mjs` — nav tree, per-page
frontmatter, content hashes, capability join, per-snippet status, and the
build identity the corpus was verified against. Never hand-edit it; every
later projection (MCP, admin console, CLI) consumes the manifest rather than
re-parsing the tree.

The same command emits [`guide-flat.generated.md`](./guide-flat.generated.md):
the capability index first, then every page exactly once in manifest nav
order. Its SHA-256 is the manifest's `contentHash`. The guide checker rejects
either generated file when stale. At server compile time, `build.rs` restamps
the embedded manifest's `buildIdentity.commit` to the exact binary build; the
checked source manifest remains the corpus-generation record.

## Freshness

Warning-only, but sound: the checker reports pages whose `authorities:`
changed between `reviewed-commit` and `HEAD` (via `git diff`). Dates are
never identity. Expired GAP review dates and check failures gate; drift
warnings don't (LLP 0061 §Design 3).

# Retrieval eval protocol

<!-- @ref LLP 0061#5-keeping-it-current-ownership-the-diary-loop-and-a-small-eval — the pinned protocol -->

The repeatable check that the guide's discovery wiring actually works: a
cold agent with a real intent finds the paved road through the guide instead
of building around it. This is the Phase 1 exit criterion and reruns after
any discovery-wiring change (the AGENTS.md pointer, the README row, the
index page, the capability index's shape).

## Fixture

A fresh agent context — same family/tier as the repo's primary authoring
agents — cold-started in a Snapback checkout at HEAD with `AGENTS.md` as the
only steer. No prior conversation, no memory of this repo's guide.

## Seed intents

At least three, across feature areas (extend, don't replace, when new areas
land):

1. **Realtime:** "Add a live-updating list of items to an app built on
   Snapback." Expected pages: `realtime/live-queries.md` (and
   `getting-started/` if starting fresh).
2. **Ephemeral:** "Let two users of my Snapback app see each other's
   cursors." Expected pages: `recipes/presence-cursors.md` or
   `realtime/ephemeral-state.md`.
3. **Auth:** "Scope a query so each signed-in user only sees their own
   rows." Expected pages: `auth/sessions-and-principals.md`,
   `recipes/hidden-hands.md`.

## Budget

The relevant guide page must be loaded within the first ~15 tool uses.

## Rubric

The run passes when the agent:

- (a) loads the relevant guide page(s) within budget;
- (b) plans or implements with the paved technique the page teaches; and
- (c) does **not** reach for the named anti-patterns — hand-wired HTTP glue
  for app data, polling a subscribable query, client-asserted identity.

## Evidence

The transcript of each run is retained under `guide/eval-runs/` (dated
subdirectory per run, one file per intent), referenced from the run's
summary note. A failed intent files a guide gap (see
[conventions](./conventions.md)) and blocks the change that triggered the
rerun until dispositioned.

## Owner and cadence

The guide's named owner (see `capabilities.md` header). Run at Phase 1 exit
and after any discovery-wiring change. Two consecutive runs with a failed
intent escalate to the Exact LLP 0365 retrieval-eval machinery per
LLP 0061's adoption triggers.

## Baseline

The failure exemplars this eval must not reproduce: diary 0010's
connection-state source-reading detour and ENG-22218's hand-wired HTTP glue.

# Sessions and principals

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](./targets.md).

The one idea (LLP 0039): **the server derives who you are; the client never
asserts it.** In sessions mode, `ctx.auth` comes only from a server-minted
session resolved at one invocation gate covering every entry path — HTTP,
WebSocket, everything. Everything this page teaches is witnessed by
`demos/card-game/tests/acceptance/authority-scope.mjs`, which runs in the
local proof.

Auth mode is per-app schema config
(`auth: { mode: 'dev' | 'sessions' }` in `defineSchema` — see
[your first backend](../getting-started/your-first-backend.md)). `dev` mode
is the trusted-local convenience where tests pass `userId:` directly;
`sessions` is the real thing below.

## Sign in: email code → session credential

The client requests a code and exchanges it. In tests, the code is read
from the server's admin-gated mailbox (a real mail sender fills that role
outside tests):

```js source=demos/card-game/tests/acceptance/authority-scope.mjs
  const requested = await client.authRequestCode(email);
```

```js source=demos/card-game/tests/acceptance/authority-scope.mjs
  const credential = await client.authExchange({
    challengeId: requested.challengeId,
    code: mailbox.code,
  });
```

From then on the client carries the session credential; `AuthCoordinator`
(from `@snapback/contract`) owns custody, refresh, and the logout barrier
for surface-based clients.

## Queries are scoped by the server, not by arguments

A protected query takes **no owner argument**. Its filter compares the stored
owner field with `authUserId()`, which the server resolves from the session:

```js source=demos/card-game/snapback/functions.mjs
  filter: [
    eq('ownerId', authUserId()),
    eq('gameId', arg('gameId')),
  ],
```

That predicate is the security boundary. For JS live queries,
`authScopeField` additionally declares which result field represents the
principal so the live matcher can reason about disjoint subscriptions; it does
not inject an ownership filter. Two signed-in users see disjoint results over
the same query:

```js source=demos/card-game/tests/acceptance/authority-scope.mjs
  const [adaResult, graceResult] = await Promise.all([
    ada.client.query('myHand', { args: { gameId } }),
    grace.client.query('myHand', { args: { gameId } }),
  ]);
  assert.deepEqual(adaResult.rows.map(({ card }) => card), ['ace-spades', 'queen-hearts']);
  assert.deepEqual(graceResult.rows.map(({ card }) => card), ['king-clubs', 'ten-diamonds']);
```

Trying to smuggle identity through the request body is rejected with a
stable code — assert on it, don't work around it:
`SNAPBACK_AUTH_BODY_AUTH_UNSUPPORTED`.

## Logout is a barrier, not a suggestion

Logging out blanks that principal's live boundaries immediately; other
principals' subscriptions are untouched:

```js source=demos/card-game/tests/acceptance/authority-scope.mjs
  await ada.client.authLogout();
  assert.deepEqual(adaSurface.boundary.current('hand'), []);
```

Offline retention of authorized data is honest too — retained rows survive
a cold boot only until the signed lease's exact deadline; see the
[hidden hands recipe](../recipes/hidden-hands.md) for the paved sequence and
[protecting data](./protecting-data.md) for connection grants, invalidation,
retry, and lease mechanics.

## Ask the server what auth is actually on

Don't guess from docs — the capability manifest's runtime facts carry
`authProgramReadiness` (a per-facet boolean projection: provider core,
shared invocation gate, connection binding, authorization invalidation,
authorized leases, session activation readiness, ...) plus the active
`AuthMode`. `GET /inspect` (public projection) and the admin inspect carry
it; teach your tooling to read it. This is the boundary rule this guide
itself follows: an auth behavior is teachable only when it has an
acceptance witness or shows as ready here.

**Partial and still an explicit guide gap:** local agent principals and scoped
grants (LLP 0055) now have real registration/grant routes, scoped-token app
invocation, the headless `AgentAuthorityFence`, and several terminal lifecycle
paths. The RFC's owner invitation/re-credentialing/revoke-all and logical
export/import work is not complete, so this guide does not present the slice as
a finished end-to-end auth product. The [capability index](../capabilities.md)
keeps it as an owned GAP until a dedicated page can teach the exact supported
subset. For the shipped local role-per-resource surface, continue to
[scoped roles and memberships](./scoped-roles.md).

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not assert identity from the client** — no `userId` in bodies, no
  owner arguments on protected queries. The server derives it or the
  request is rejected.
- **Do not build auth UI against unwitnessed surface.** Check
  `authProgramReadiness` / the capability index instead of assuming a
  route's existence means its behavior is on.
- **Do not treat retained offline data as unconditionally readable** — the
  lease deadline is exact and enforced client-side too.

# Protecting live and retained data

> **Local target only.** These guarantees are witnessed on the canonical
> Ibex/SQLite target. Hosted auth is not available; see
> [target honesty](./targets.md).

Start with [sessions and principals](./sessions-and-principals.md) to sign in
and scope a query, or the [hidden-hands recipe](../recipes/hidden-hands.md) for
the shortest end-to-end example. This page is the systematic reference for
what happens after private data becomes live or retained.

## Check the negotiated capability, not route existence

`authProgramReadiness` in inspect reports separate build/runtime facts:
provider core, the shared invocation gate, staged mode, connection binding,
two-phase revocation, `AuthCoordinator`, authorization invalidation, authority
descriptors, authorized leases, and derived session-activation readiness.

The authenticated `client.authSession()` projection then reports what this
exact connection may use:

- `availability.onlineRequestResponse`;
- `availability.authScopedLive`, including the required invalidation protocol;
- `availability.retainedReads`, requiring invalidation **and** authorized
  leases; and
- `availability.queuedReplay`, requiring authority descriptors.

In sessions mode, an auth-scoped live subscription is admitted only when both
server and client negotiate `authInvalidationProtocol: 1`. Retained reads also
require `authorizedLeaseProtocol: 1`. A route present behind an unavailable
facet is not a supported capability.

## Connection grants bind live work to authority

The string your app supplies as `connectionId` is a logical sharing label. On
open, Snapback returns a granted id, a secret connection token, and the exact
authorization-invalidation expectation:

```js source=demos/_kit/tests/auth-invalidation-client.mjs
      return response({
        connectionId: 'granted-auth',
        connectionToken: 'sct_auth',
        authorizationInvalidation: {
          protocolVersion: 1,
          issuerId,
          connectionGeneration: 2,
          authorization,
          versionStream: 'stream-A',
        },
      });
```

That grant is authority, not a bearer-shaped routing convenience. It is bound
to one anonymous authorization stream, one exact session generation, or one
scoped service-principal authority plus its exact token/deadline carrier. The
service form keeps the durable resolved authority separate from the token and
its service-publication fence, so ending one token cannot widen or silently
rebind the grant. Every live subscribe/resume, outbox drain, ephemeral act, and
publication validates the grant token and binding at its final effect fence.
HTTP sends the token in `x-snapback-connection-token`; browser WebSockets use
the negotiated `snapback.connection-token.*` subprotocol.

An auth transition clears cached grants and reconnects under a fresh grant.
Never persist, copy between clients, log, or manually reuse a connection
token. Let one `SnapbackClient` multiplex consumers that intentionally share a
logical connection label.

## Authorization change is a persistent obligation

Logout is one visible case, but the barrier also covers permission or
membership changes, coarse authorization-version advances, activation/reset
boundaries, and protected ephemeral-room authority changes. A change that may
shrink a result raises a revisioned obligation against the exact live/query
scope.

The reachable-client sequence is:

1. The client receives the obligation and synchronously applies its maximum
   disposition—normally `quarantine`, sometimes terminal `delete`.
2. Live rows blank; retained reads block; optimistic/outbox custody for that
   scope suspends. Ordinary live frames cannot repopulate it.
3. The server resolves with a fresh satisfying snapshot or trusted terminal
   denial tied to the same scope/revision/witness.
4. The client atomically commits the disposition, snapshot or tombstone,
   queue/store resolution, and local boundary.
5. Only after that commit does it acknowledge the opaque resolution token.

The kit test pins the order:

```js source=demos/_kit/tests/auth-invalidation-client.mjs
  assert.deepEqual(order.slice(0, 3), [
    'queue-apply:1',
    'queue-resolve:1',
    'ack:ack_1',
  ]);
```

A lost delivery is safe because obligations are level-triggered state, not
one-shot events: connection open, subscribe/resume, drains, and heartbeats
re-project unresolved work. A stale acknowledgement re-quarantines; a duplicate
successful acknowledgement is idempotent. A queue/store failure leaves the
boundary blank and stale until the exact obligation re-fires with valid proof.

Protected ephemeral rooms use the same principle: affected sinks quiesce before
the authorization-changing commit becomes visible, then fresh room
reauthorization either admits the successor generation or revokes it.

## Retry is bounded and explicit

Automatic satisfying resnapshot attempts are bounded. Exhaustion leaves the
scope quarantined; reconnect or subscribe does not reset the episode. The
`POST /live/authorization-invalidation/manual-retry` operation is an
authority-checked recovery control that requires the current connection,
scope, and a fresh idempotency id. It is not an ordinary UI retry button and
cannot replace an episode before automatic attempts are exhausted.

Use normal client/barrier recovery first. Operator or acceptance tooling should
invoke manual retry only for a surfaced unresolved episode, keep the same
current authority, and treat capacity, clock-rollback, stale-scope, and denial
diagnostics as fail-closed outcomes.

## Authorized leases bound unreachable honest clients

An offline client cannot receive an obligation. Therefore every readable
auth-scoped retained snapshot needs a server-issued `AuthorizedLease`, bound to
the exact principal, authorization version, app/data version stream, active
artifacts, client store, query key, and query-instance id.

Lease acquisition is one full revalidation, not a heartbeat:

1. The client durably reserves a fresh `leaseRequestId` and records the request
   start against its clock high-water.
2. `authorizedLeaseQuery` performs the full query. At one server commit-order
   boundary, Snapback proves the app-data head, authority, active artifacts,
   and absence of a pending invalidation obligation.
3. The response carries the snapshot and lease together. The client validates
   its closed shape/bindings and atomically commits rows, witness, exact lease
   bytes/hash, and derived deadline before render.

```js source=packages/snapback-client/index.mjs
    return this.#req('POST', `/query/${encodeURIComponent(name)}/authorized-lease`, {
      args,
      auth: SnapbackClient.auth(userId),
      read_set: readSet,
      leaseRequestId,
      clientStoreId: namespace.clientStoreId,
      queryKey: namespace.queryKey,
      queryInstanceId: namespace.queryInstanceId,
    }, undefined, { expectedAuthorityCapture: authorityCapture });
```

V1 defaults to 24 hours and has a 24-hour hard maximum; configuration may only
shorten it. Session/provider expiries clamp the server deadline. The client
derives its deadline from the request-start clock plus the server-issued
duration, so network delay shortens validity rather than extending it.

Heartbeat, delta delivery, reconnect, acknowledgement, mutation, session
refresh, or presenting an old lease never renews it. Renewal is another full
query and atomic proof. At or beyond the exact client deadline—or on clock
rollback, malformed/missing lease, mismatched identity/witness/instance, stale
activation, or invalid request reservation—the store commits delete-before-read
for that query instance.

The server verifies the lease MAC because only it owns the key. The client
validates structure and bindings and hashes the exact bytes for custody
corruption detection; it cannot cryptographically authenticate a server MAC.

## Understand the threat boundary

The lease bounds an honest device that is temporarily unreachable. It is not
anti-tamper: a hostile client can alter its clock or read bytes it already owns.
If adversarial-client access to retained private bytes is in scope, do not
enable retained reads. A legitimate revocation may remain visible to an honest
offline device until its lease deadline; that is the explicit local-first
product tradeoff.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not handle invalidation as an edge event.** Preserve the obligation
  until committed resolution and acknowledgement.
- **Do not ACK before the boundary/store commit.** Delivery is not discharge.
- **Do not render quarantined rows or allow ordinary frames to refill them.**
- **Do not treat reconnect as manual retry or lease renewal.**
- **Do not cache authorized rows outside the lease-enforcing client store.**
- **Do not infer hosted guarantees from the local readiness projection.**

# Scoped roles and memberships

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](./targets.md).

Snapback models authorization roles as rows with a system-recognized shape:
principal, optional resource, and role. The roster stays live app data, while
the host owns the transition checks, query semi-join, denial, invalidation, and
provenance. Roles are not copied into session claims.

The shipped v1 lane is for online queries, live queries, and mutations. It does
not yet make membership-gated results retainable offline, emit incremental
semi-join deltas, or support hosted targets.

## Privacy posture and reachable operations

Membership backing rows are fully private in v1: application code cannot list
them, ask whether one exists, or obtain their row ids, and `insert` returns
`null`. That posture deliberately forecloses administrator-driven
id-addressed `setRole`, `remove`, and `patch` in ordinary app handlers. The
methods exist for trusted migration/import contexts that already possess a
row id; the private app surface does not mint one. Do not source-dive for an
escape hatch—the absence is the security contract.

| Operation under the private v1 posture | Reachable app path |
| --- | --- |
| create a resource plus its first holder | `bootstrap(...)` (resource scope) |
| add self or another principal | declared `insert` transition; returns no row id |
| accept/decline/change/remove the caller's own seat | `setSelfRole`, `removeSelf`, or `patchSelf` |
| administrator changes/removes/patches another existing seat | foreclosed: requires a private row id |
| read/list/sync the roster or test another seat's existence | foreclosed: use `memberOf`/`hasRole` semi-joins or `requireRole` |

For invitations, keep the pending invitation in an ordinary app-data table
whose privacy policy fits the product. The invitee consumes that record and
performs a declaration-authorized self `insert` into the final membership
role. Alternatively, use a membership `pendingRole` only when the invitee can
finish through a self-addressed transition, as the app-wide example below
does. Do not imply that the inviter can promote the private row later: it
cannot obtain that row's id.

## Declare an app-wide role set

An app-scoped declaration omits the resource axis. This demo supports open
self-join plus member-issued invitations that only the invited principal can
accept or decline:

```js source=demos/rbac/snapback/schema.mjs
export const appMembers = defineTable({
  userId: v.principal(),
  role: v.string(),
}).membership({
  principal: 'userId',
  role: 'role',
  roles: ['member', 'admin'],
  pendingRoles: ['invited'],
  scope: 'app',
  provenance: 'full',
  transitions: [
    { op: 'insert', by: ['none'], target: 'self', to: ['member'] },
    { op: 'insert', by: ['member'], target: 'other', to: ['invited'] },
    { op: 'setRole', by: ['self'], target: 'self', from: ['invited'], to: ['member'] },
    { op: 'remove', by: ['self'], target: 'self', from: ['invited', 'member'] },
  ],
});
```

The transition grammar is closed. Each operation declares its allowed caller
class, self/other target, old/new roles, and—for inserts or patches—extra
fields. Unknown keys, undeclared roles, unreachable combinations, and empty
role sets fail artifact generation or activation. Runtime evaluation derives
the principal and current membership inside the write transaction; the caller
cannot supply either fact as authority.

For a role per resource, add a required resource field typed with the nominal
table id. `v.id('events')` is not interchangeable with another string-shaped
id:

```js source=packages/snapback-codegen/rbac-authoring.test.mjs
export const eventMembers = defineTable({
  eventId: v.id('events'),
  userId: v.principal(),
  role: v.string(),
  joinedAt: v.integer(),
}).membership({
  id: 'eventMembers',
  principal: 'userId',
  resource: 'eventId',
  role: 'role',
  roles: ['host', 'guest'],
  pendingRoles: ['invited'],
  bootstrapRole: 'host',
  lastHolder: { protect: 'host' },
  incidental: ['joinedAt'],
  provenance: 'full',
  transitions: [],
});
```

Codegen derives `resourceTable` from that validator and carries the nominal
type into the function artifact. An argument or row-field helper bound to
`Id<'organizations'>` is rejected before publication when the declaration
requires `Id<'events'>`.

## Gate a query with the declaration

Use helpers on the exported membership table, never a global role string.
`memberOf()` admits any non-pending role; `hasRole(resource, ...roles)` admits
only the named roles, including a pending role when explicitly named.

For app scope, omit the resource. Snapback binds the host-owned app singleton:

```js source=demos/rbac/snapback/functions.mjs
export const listAnnouncements = defineLiveQuery({
  auth: 'authenticated',
  table: 'announcements',
  args: {},
  membership: [appMembers.memberOf()],
  order: [asc('_createdAt')],
});
```

For resource scope, pass exactly one of
`membershipResource.arg('eventId')` or
`membershipResource.rowField('eventId')`. The predicate is an authoritative
membership semi-join, not an optimistic client expression. It records an
ordinary captured database dependency even when no membership row exists, so
joining can wake a previously empty live result.

That dependency also means a membership-filtered query cannot declare
`authorityIndependent: true`. Codegen rejects the combination before writing
artifacts; public routing does not make a roster-dependent result invariant
across principals.

Membership tables are private authorization backing in v1. There is no
application-returning `ctx.permissions.*.get()` and a normal query cannot use
the roster as an existence oracle.

## Check a role inside a transaction

Query and mutation handlers receive declaration-qualified permission helpers.
App scope uses `null` as the imperative resource value:

```js source=demos/rbac/snapback/handlers.mjs
  async postAnnouncement(ctx, args) {
    await ctx.permissions.appMembers.requireRole(null, 'member', 'admin');
    return await ctx.db.insert('announcements', {
      authorId: ctx.auth.userId,
      message: args.message,
    });
  },
```

A failed check is always `SNAPBACK_AUTH_PERMISSION_DENIED` with invariant
public details `{ kind: 'role' }`. It reveals neither whether the resource nor
membership exists. The denial is host-owned and remains terminal even if app
JavaScript catches the thrown error. Actions have no transactional read set,
so `ctx.permissions` is deliberately unavailable there.

## Change membership through generated methods

Only mutation handlers receive `ctx.membership`. Its `insert`, id-addressed
`setRole`/`remove`/`patch`, and self-addressed
`setSelfRole`/`removeSelf`/`patchSelf` methods submit a host-owned command
evaluated against the declaration:

```js source=demos/rbac/snapback/handlers.mjs
  async joinApp(ctx) {
    await ctx.membership.appMembers.insert({
      userId: ctx.auth.userId,
      role: 'member',
    });
    return null;
  },
```

App code does not need the private roster row id for its own transitions. App
scope omits the resource argument; resource scope passes its branded resource
id:

```js source=demos/rbac/snapback/handlers.mjs
  async acceptInvite(ctx) {
    await ctx.membership.appMembers.setSelfRole('member');
    return null;
  },

  async leaveApp(ctx) {
    await ctx.membership.appMembers.removeSelf();
    return null;
  },
```

The host resolves only the effective principal's row, returns no id, and then
runs the same declared transition matrix. A missing own row is
`SNAPBACK_MEMBERSHIP_SELF_NOT_FOUND`; no helper reveals whether anyone else has
a row. The id-addressed forms are not an administrator authoring path for the
private v1 roster; only a trusted migration/import context outside the normal
app surface can already hold such an id.

Generic `ctx.db` and HostPlan writes to a membership table fail with
`SNAPBACK_MEMBERSHIP_RAW_WRITE_DENIED`; handler convention is not the security
boundary. Mark any function that can create durable authority with
`authorityCreating: true`. That marker becomes part of delegated-agent consent
and requires full membership provenance.

A resource declaration with `bootstrapRole` also gets
`ctx.membership.<declaration>.bootstrap(resourceValues)`. It returns the fresh,
branded resource id and atomically inserts both the resource and a membership
that seats the server-derived effective principal in the bootstrap role. A
`lastHolder` declaration relies on this path: creating the protected resource
without its initial eligible holder is refused.

A JavaScript mutation dedicated to that one bootstrap operation may set
`authorityCreating: false` even though its declared writes include the resource
and membership tables. Bootstrap cannot name a different principal, so a
delegated agent seats its effective user rather than itself. The runtime still
rejects every non-bootstrap membership operation from such an unconsented
wrapper; a mutation that can perform bootstrap *and* ordinary membership
changes must use `authorityCreating: true`.

The generated TypeScript surface brands principals and resource ids, emits
closed role unions and insert/patch values, exposes `GeneratedPermissions` to
queries and mutations, and exposes `GeneratedMembership` only to mutations.

## Keep the authorization composition seams aligned

An authorized live effect is valid only while all of these captured facts
still describe the same operation:

- **coordinator epoch** — which authenticated authority generation owns the client;
- **queue generation** — which durable outbox generation may replay;
- **artifact identity** — the schema/function bundle whose declarations were checked;
- **principal scope** — effective user or scoped service-principal tuple;
- **descriptor** — the exact query/mutation plus args and authorization dependence;
- **query lease** — the live subscription generation allowed to receive rows.

Treat the set as one composition boundary. A principal/token/grant transition
must close or blank the old query lease before a successor publishes; queued
work must compare both its authority capture and store generation; generated
descriptors must match the active artifact hashes. The Contract adapter and
packaged client perform these comparisons. App code should not cache a roster
answer, splice a new bearer into an old client, or reuse a live handle across a
coordinator transition.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not store roles in session claims.** Membership rows are the current
  authority; copying them creates stale credentials.
- **Do not accept a plain string where `v.id(table)` is required.** Preserve
  the nominal resource binding through arguments and row fields.
- **Do not query or sync the roster to make an authorization decision.** Use a
  declaration-bound predicate or `ctx.permissions.requireRole`.
- **Do not design administrator promotion/removal around private membership
  row ids.** V1 intentionally does not make those ids reachable; use app-data
  invitations plus a self transition, or choose a product flow that does not
  require administrator mutation of an existing private seat.
- **Do not create an app-data roster-id mirror just to leave or accept.** Use
  the declaration's self-addressed write methods.
- **Do not write membership rows through `ctx.db` or a generic HostPlan.** Use
  mutation-only generated membership methods and declare every transition.
- **Do not create a `lastHolder`-protected resource with `ctx.db.insert`.** Use
  the declaration's atomic `bootstrap()` method.
- **Do not use `ctx.permissions` in an action or retain a role-gated result
  offline.** Neither has the transactional/lease proof required by v1.

# Targets — what each one claims

Snapback is deliberately honest about which guarantees belong to which
execution target. Guide pages carry `targets:` frontmatter for exactly this
reason; this page is the map those banners point to.

## Local (Ibex + SQLite) — the canonical dev/test target

The full local server (LLP 0002) is where every guide technique on a
`targets: [local]` page holds: server-authoritative mutations with one
commit version and read-set validation, live queries over the durable lane,
ephemeral realtime, and local sessions-mode auth with server-derived
principals, connection-bound live grants, auth-invalidation barriers, and
signed authorized-lease offline retention. The systematic local contract is
[protecting live and retained data](./protecting-data.md).

**What the local target deliberately does NOT claim** (LLP 0060; the
README's must-not-claim posture): these are local-target guarantees, not
hosted-auth readiness. The local target reports no target-owned external
TLS, no trusted effective-source derivation, no shared authentication
throttle, no multi-replica invalidation, and no sender-constrained browser
credential. Hosted auth is honestly **disabled** on the local bearer
target rather than half-claimed.

## Cloudflare — the hosted proof, as far as it is real

The Cloudflare target (LLP 0014/0040/0049) is a working proof — the All
Aboard demo runs live on it with Durable Objects storage, deploy-time
secrets, gated action egress, and settled idle-to-zero evidence. It is a
narrow proof, not a paved product target: treat any technique on a page
without `cloudflare` in its `targets:` as unverified there, and treat
hosted auth as absent until LLP 0060's contract is implemented and
witnessed. Deployment, secret, egress, hibernation, and non-claim details are
in [deploying the Cloudflare proof](../deploying/cloudflare.md).

## How to check instead of trusting prose

A running server states its own capabilities: `GET /inspect` carries the
capability manifest with runtime facts including `authProgramReadiness`
and the active auth mode. When a page's claim and a server's report
disagree, the server is right and the page has drifted — file a guide gap
(see [conventions](../conventions.md)).

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not generalize a local guarantee into a hosted claim.** The gap is
  the product's honesty boundary, and this guide inherits it mechanically.
- **Do not ship a browser bearer credential to real users on the local
  target and call it auth.** That configuration exists for local
  development; LLP 0060 documents why it must not be marketed as more.

# Agent principals and scoped grants

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](./targets.md).

An agent is a service principal with its own credential. It does not borrow a
human session bearer. A grant gives that principal a closed set of function
scopes, and each short-lived scoped token names the agent credential,
credential generation, grant, and token carrier. The server still applies
ordinary auth requirements, row scoping, and
[roles](./scoped-roles.md); a token never bypasses those gates.

## Pair an already registered agent

Registration is an owner or invitation flow that creates the agent and returns
its one-time credential. Keep that credential outside source, logs, generated
artifacts, and model output. Pairing then delegates a user's authority without
letting the agent name or enumerate users:

1. A signed-in user calls `POST /auth/pairing-codes` and conveys the short-lived
   code out of band.
2. The agent calls `POST /auth/agents/pair` with `credential`,
   `pairingRequestId`, `pairingCode`, and the exact `requestedScopes`.
3. The user inspects `GET /auth/grant-requests` and approves or denies the
   pending request. Approval displays the agent, provenance, scopes, expiry,
   and owner-assumption disclosure.
4. The agent polls `POST /auth/agents/token` with its credential and
   `pairingRequestId`. `SNAPBACK_AUTH_GRANT_PENDING` means wait; the
   non-enumerating `SNAPBACK_AUTH_GRANT_INVALID` means stop.

The token response contains `tokenId`, `grantId`, `credentialId`,
`credentialGeneration`, expiry, canonical scopes, and the bearer. Re-polling an
approved request rotates the first token; it does not retrieve old plaintext.

## Choose scopes deliberately

An explicit function scope binds a stable function id, kind, manifest basis,
and whether the function can create authority. A tier scope such as
`{ tier: "query" }` follows the current manifest and therefore includes later
queries. Prefer explicit function scopes when deployment must not silently
expand reach. `authorityCreating` operations never join a tier implicitly.

Delegated grants expire, at most 90 days. Renewal is a new consent. Autonomous
grants come only from the app's registration template on production-like
postures; the local operator mint exists for development and testing, not as a
production escape hatch.

## Fence token custody before doing work

Construct `AgentAuthorityFence` from the token response plus the registered
agent actor id, then pass it to `SnapbackClient` as `agentAuthority`. The client
probes `/auth/session`, verifies the exact service-principal descriptor, and
only publishes results while the captured credential-generation/grant/token
carrier is still current. Use filesystem custody for a long-running Node agent;
use the volatile fence only for a bounded process.

Never return or serialize the bearer as an operation result. Rotation uses
`replaceAgentCredential(...)`; revocation or terminal auth loss synchronously
cuts publication and either retires the carrier or deletes the durable grant
tuple according to the server's classified disposition.

## Revoke and verify

An agent can use `/auth/agents/revoke-self` and `/auth/agents/rotate` for its own
credential lifecycle. A signed-in grantor manages grants through
`/auth/grants`; operator-only lifecycle actions stay on the host-operations
plane. After a mutation, verify through a query or live snapshot under the same
fenced authority. The packaged acceptance witness in
`packages/snapback-app-cli/package.test.mjs` exercises discovery, pairing,
scoped custody, mutation, subscription, and verification without exposing the
token in its returned result.

## Anti-patterns

- Do not put an admin token into an app agent; host operations and app data are
  separate authority planes.
- Do not let an agent choose an effective user id in a request body.
- Do not treat a tier grant as deployment-pinned.
- Do not persist bearer plaintext in the durable custody ledger or print it in
  diagnostics.
- Do not retry `SNAPBACK_AUTH_GRANT_INVALID` as if it were pending.

# Queries

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

A query is a read-only function over one consistent database snapshot. Its
result is `{ rows, version }`: the rows and reported version come from the
same pinned snapshot, so an author never has to reconcile a result with a
separately sampled version.

## Choose declarative or JavaScript execution

Declarative queries spell out the table, arguments, predicates, ordering, and
index in the function definition:

```js source=demos/todo/snapback/functions.mjs
export const listTodosOnce = defineQuery({
  table: 'todos',
  args: {},
  filter: [eq('userId', authUserId())],
  order: [asc('_createdAt')],
  index: 'by_user',
});
```

`defineJsQuery` and `defineJsLiveQuery` instead name a bundled handler and
declare the tables they may read. The handler uses the bounded `ctx.db`
surface:

```js source=demos/todo/snapback/handlers.mjs
  async listTodos(ctx) {
    return await ctx.db
      .query('todos')
      .withIndex('by_user')
      .eq('userId', ctx.auth.userId)
      .order('_createdAt', 'asc')
      .collect();
  },
```

Use the declarative form when the plan vocabulary expresses the query. Use a
JS handler for bounded logic the plan cannot express. Both styles return the
same public query envelope and must use declared indexes for author-facing
lookup paths.

Every JS query handler returns an **array of rows**, including point reads:
return `[]` for missing or `[row]` for present. Returning a single object fails
with `SNAPBACK_HANDLER_RESULT_INVALID`; the diagnostic names whether the
declaration is a `query` or `live query` and includes its function id.

## Read one snapshot

The local target pins one transaction for the whole query invocation. The
normal file-backed read lane uses the WAL reader pool; direct-library,
live-subscription, and in-memory fallback lanes pin the serialized connection
instead. Every `get`, indexed query, membership witness, and terminal `version`
observes that same snapshot. Queries never write; a write attempt is a typed
refusal.

Inside a mutation, `ctx.db` layers the mutation's own buffered writes over each
logical storage read. Those reads become commit dependencies, described in
[mutations](./mutations.md). Each logical read pins its reported head and rows
together; buffered-query overlays capture the exact overfetch and touched rows
they consumed before commit validation.

The returned `version` is an exact integer in
`0..=Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`. A malformed, negative, or out-of-range durable
cursor fails closed instead of being rounded, wrapped, or replaced with zero.

## Scope on the server

Put authorization predicates in the query, not in client arguments or UI
filters. `authUserId()` in declarative plans and `ctx.auth.userId` in JS
handlers are server-derived. For sessions-mode details, see
[sessions and principals](../auth/sessions-and-principals.md).

## Make a query live only when needed

`defineQuery` is callable but not subscribable. `defineLiveQuery` and
`defineJsLiveQuery` opt into the analyzable live surface. A client that tries
to subscribe to an ordinary query receives
`SNAPBACK_FUNCTION_NOT_LIVE`; Snapback never silently converts it into a
polling contract. See [live queries](../realtime/live-queries.md).

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not sample rows and version separately.** The query envelope already
  binds them to one snapshot.
- **Do not filter private rows in the client.** Put server-derived ownership
  in the query predicate.
- **Do not omit an available index.** A declarative `index` or JS
  `withIndex` makes the intended lookup explicit and portable.
- **Do not mark every query live.** Ordinary queries stay ordinary; opt into
  live delivery only when the UI needs subscription semantics.

# Mutations

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

A mutation makes snapshot-atomic logical reads, buffers writes, validates its
captured dependencies, and commits once. It does not hold one SQLite read
transaction across arbitrary asynchronous handler work; commit-time OCC rejects
relevant drift between reads. Every row changed by the commit receives the
same monotonic version. A rejected mutation commits nothing.

## Define the write boundary

The JS form declares arguments, handler source, and its possible writes:

```js source=demos/todo/snapback/functions.mjs
export const createTodo = defineJsMutation({
  args: { title: v.string() },
  source: 'handlers.mjs',
  exportName: 'createTodo',
  writes: ['todos'],
});
```

The handler writes only through `ctx.db`. Server-owned ids, timestamps, and
row versions are not arguments and are never authored by the handler:

```js source=demos/todo/snapback/handlers.mjs
    return await ctx.db.insert('todos', {
      title,
      completed: false,
      userId: ctx.auth.userId,
    });
```

`defineMutation` is the declarative twin: compose `insert`, `patch`,
`delete`, conditions, and a declared return binding without running a JS
handler.

A mutation that declares a write to a `permissionBacking` table is generated
with `authorityCreating: true`. Authors may explicitly mark an opaque mutation
conservatively, but cannot clear a derived marker. Under the partial local
agent-auth slice this requires grant consent at admission, and the host still
enforces the exact permission-backing write dynamically.

## Consume the structured result

Successful direct mutations return one closed envelope:
`version`, `changed_count`, `result`, an optional deterministic
`ctx_ledger`, and the terminal `receipt`. The todo acceptance proves the
created id, changed count, and server-owned row fields together:

```js source=demos/todo/tests/acceptance/headless.mjs
    const created = await db.mutate(api.createTodo, { args: { title: 'Buy milk' }, userId: ADA });
    assert(typeof created.result === 'string' && created.result.length > 0, 'no id returned');
    assertEqual(created.changed_count, 1, 'changed_count');
    const rows = (await db.query(api.listTodos, { userId: ADA })).rows;
```

An error is a structured `SNAPBACK_*` diagnostic. A rejected queued mutation
still has a terminal receipt on the error envelope so the client store can
settle it without guessing. A confirmed receipt always carries a non-null
durable `snapshotVersion`; `null` is allowed only for a rejected invocation
whose durable cursor could not be read safely.

## Preserve invariants with read sets

JS mutation reads are captured by the server. Declarative host-plan mutations
that depend on an earlier client observation carry that explicit
`readSet`. At commit, Snapback validates the exact row or predicate
dependencies. If a concurrent writer changed a dependency, the whole mutation
is rejected as `SNAPBACK_MUTATION_CONFLICT`:

```js source=demos/todo/tests/acceptance/headless.mjs
    const err = await assertThrows(
      () => db.mutate(api.setCompleted, {
        args: { id, completed: false },
        userId: ADA,
        readSet: [{ table: 'todos', id, version: observed }],
      }),
      'SNAPBACK_MUTATION_CONFLICT',
      'expected conflict',
    );
```

Treat that diagnostic as an invariant failure to reconcile, not as permission
to force a last-writer-wins commit. Predicate-shaped captured reads are
validated at predicate granularity, so unrelated writes do not spuriously
conflict.

## Declare structural uniqueness

For one-row-per-key application invariants, declare a true unique index instead
of scanning in the handler:

```js source=demos/shindig/snapback/schema.mjs
    .index('by_user', ['userId'])
    .index('by_event', ['eventId'])
    .index('by_event_user', ['eventId', 'userId'], { unique: true })
    .sync(),
```

Unique indexes may be compound. Every key field must be required in v1 so the
constraint is total across SQLite and Postgres. Duplicate inserts that reach
the serialized write boundary race at the constraint: exactly one wins, every
loser commits nothing and receives `SNAPBACK_UNIQUE_CONSTRAINT_VIOLATION`. A
larger mutation may still fail earlier at an authorization or stale-reservation
boundary, also without committing. Snapback does not currently ship `upsert`;
keep duplicate-as-error flows as inserts and handle the unique diagnostic.

## One commit, one version

All affected rows share the mutation's `version`; no-op writes do not advance
it. Durable live delivery is produced from the committed write set, so clients
never observe a partial mutation. The version is a logical ordering within one
app database, not a wall-clock timestamp. It is an exact integer in
`0..=Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`. The maximum commit is usable, but an operation
that needs its successor fails before writing with
`SNAPBACK_STORAGE_VERSION_EXHAUSTED`; never round or synthesize a cursor.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not implement read-then-write invariants as two unrelated requests.**
  Read inside the JS mutation or carry the explicit host-plan baseline.
- **Do not scan to emulate a unique compound key.** Declare a unique index;
  read sets are conflict detection, not a substitute for structural uniqueness.
- **Do not swallow `SNAPBACK_MUTATION_CONFLICT`.** Reconcile or ask the user;
  blind retry may violate the invariant that caused the read.
- **Do not set `_id`, `_version`, `_createdAt`, or `_updatedAt`.**
  They are server-owned.
- **Do not infer success from HTTP status alone.** Consume the result,
  diagnostic, and terminal receipt envelope.

# Actions and outbound fetch

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

An action is the non-transactional function class for external I/O and
longer-running orchestration. It may fetch only when the deployment enables
outbound actions, receives only the config entries named by `uses`, and
commits durable state by calling a mutation.

## Declare the powers the action needs

All Aboard's feed action declares typed arguments, its JS handler, the one
config pool it may read, and the tables mutations it invokes can write:

```js source=demos/all-aboard/snapback/functions.mjs
export const refreshFeed = defineAction({
  args: {
    trigger: v.optional(v.string()),
    source: v.optional(v.string()),
    feedUrl: v.optional(v.string()),
    // Testing knob (short-cadence acceptance rigs): lowers the upstream-poll
    // budget window; clamped so it can never RAISE the 180s production budget.
    pollBudgetMs: v.optional(v.integer()),
  },
  js: { source: 'handlers.mjs', exportName: 'refreshFeed' },
  // @ref LLP 0036#declared-configuration-in-the-manifest — D8: the grant that
  // hands the live fetch its rotating key via ctx.secrets.
  uses: ['caltrainFeed'],
  writes: ['trainStatus', 'liveDepartures', 'feedRefreshState'],
});
```

`uses` is an allowlist, not documentation. Codegen rejects unknown entries,
and `ctx.secrets` refuses an entry the action was not granted. Declare values
and configure deployments as described in
[secrets and config](../operating/secrets-and-config.md).

For the partial local agent-auth slice, codegen also derives
`authorityCreating: true` when an action or mutation declares a write to a
`permissionBacking` table; an opaque path may conservatively set the boolean
explicitly. This is an admission signal, not the security boundary: the host
rechecks the resolved grant's exact consent at the permission-backing write.

## Keep network I/O outside the transaction

Actions do not get `ctx.db`. Fetch or compute first, then call a named
mutation through `ctx.runMutation`; that mutation owns the atomic durable
commit and live fan-out:

```js source=demos/all-aboard/snapback/handlers.mjs
      const snapshot = await fetchCaltrainSnapshot(ctx, args || {});
      return await ctx.runMutation('applyLiveFeedSnapshot', {
        trigger,
        source: '511-siri-stop-monitoring',
        delays: snapshot.delays,
        departures: snapshot.departures,
```

This split prevents a slow or failed network request from holding the write
lane. Nested mutations inherit the action's server-resolved authority; they do
not accept a replacement identity.

## Enable egress deliberately

The local runtime denies `fetch` by default. Enable it explicitly with
`SNAPBACK_OUTBOUND_ACTIONS=1` for the deployment/process that should have
egress. Queries and mutations remain denied even in that runtime:

```js source=demos/all-aboard/tests/acceptance/egress.mjs
  await suite.check('a query in the same runtime is still denied fetch and has no ctx.secrets', async () => {
    const { rows } = await dbOn.query('queryProbe', {});
    assert(/AMBIENT_CAPABILITY_DENIED/.test(rows[0].fetchState), `query fetch should be denied, got: ${rows[0].fetchState}`);
    assertEqual(rows[0].secretsState, 'undefined', 'queries get no config surface');
```

Action wall-clock limits and the detached watchdog still apply. A timed-out
action cannot commit late, and a later invocation gets an isolated worker.

## Treat fetched text as data

Egress does not make an action a general-purpose code loader. Direct or
indirect `eval`, every Function-family string constructor (including
constructor walks and reflective calls), and WebAssembly are unavailable at
the runtime boundary. The same rule applies on the local Ibex engine and the
Workerd target. Codegen reports the obvious source forms early, but the engine
policy is what prevents aliases from bypassing the rule.

Do not fetch JavaScript, templates intended for evaluation, or remote policy
code. Parse a response as validated data and pass only typed values to a named
mutation. This keeps the manifest's bundle hash truthful: an action may use its
declared secret and egress authority, but fetched bytes never inherit its
`ctx.runMutation` authority as executable code.

## Handle failure as data only when the product means it

An action may return a structured fallback result when fallback is an explicit
product behavior, as All Aboard does for recorded data. Otherwise throw: the
action error remains a structured diagnostic envelope. Never convert
configuration, permission, or timeout failures into a false success merely to
keep a UI quiet.

Await or return every asynchronous branch whose outcome matters. The runtime
treats an unhandled detached rejection as a handler failure; it cannot be
reclassified as successful settlement by replacing reachable Promise hooks.

## Stream a response

Consuming an upstream response incrementally — an AI token stream, a large
export — is its own bounded surface with its own limits, attempt control
plane, and diagnostic codes. See
[streamed actions](./streamed-actions.md) for the whole pattern:
`ctx.fetchStream`, the one-pull-per-cursor reader, the
`ctx.streamAttempt` lease/settlement surface, the v1 limits (1 MiB total,
16 KiB reads, 64 KiB buffering, 30 s wall, 5 s idle, 4 cursors, ten
progress commits per second), and every `SNAPBACK_ACTION_STREAM_*` refusal.
Stream diagnostics name this section as their repair anchor; the page above
is the repair.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not fetch inside a query or mutation.** The ambient-capability gate
  refuses it, and transactions must not wait on the network.
- **Do not pass API keys in action arguments.** Declare config and grant it
  with `uses`.
- **Do not write durable state directly from an action.** Call a mutation so
  validation, receipts, and live delivery share one commit.
- **Do not enable egress globally as a convenience.** Turn it on only for the
  deployment that needs actions with network access.
- **Do not evaluate fetched text.** Parse and validate it as data; dynamic
  source compilation is denied even for egress-enabled actions.
- **Do not launch unobserved Promise chains.** Await or return them so their
  failure remains part of the handler's explicit result.

---

# Scheduled execution with cron

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

Cron jobs are generated manifest entries that ask the target scheduler to run
an **action**. The action may perform I/O and calls mutations for durable
effects, so scheduled writes use the same atomic commit and live-delivery path
as user-triggered work.

## Define the job

All Aboard declares one demand-gated interval:

```js source=demos/all-aboard/snapback/functions.mjs
export const caltrainCron = defineCron({
  warmPoll: {
    // jitter:false because the 180s cadence is a fixed product interval for a
    // single demand-gated app; no thundering-herd concern (LLP 0028 §Jitter).
    schedule: { everyMs: 180_000, jitter: false },
    action: 'refreshFeed',
    activation: { kind: 'WhileLive', whileLive: ['liveTrainStatus'] },
  },
});
```

The complete authoring inventory for each job:

- `schedule`: exactly one of `everyMs` (local floor 1,000 ms) or a
  five-field `cron` expression;
- `action`: the name of a declared action; authenticated-only actions are
  rejected because the scheduler runs with system authority;
- `enabled`: defaults to `true`;
- `activation`: always (default) or `whileLive` over named live queries;
- `jitter` / `jitterMaxMs`: jitter defaults on; opt out only for a
  product-fixed cadence with no herd concern;
- `overlapPolicy`: defaults to `NoOverlap`;
- `retryPolicy`: defaults to `{ mode: 'NextTick' }`.

Codegen validates job names, schedules, action existence/kind, and the
auth-requirement boundary before the server loads the manifest.

## Gate polling on real demand

`whileLive` keeps a polling job inactive when nobody subscribes to the
declared query. The first subscription arms it; the last disconnect makes it
inactive again:

```js source=demos/all-aboard/tests/acceptance/cron.mjs
  // Subscribing to the declared live query arms the job (whileLive activation).
  const live = await db.liveQuery('liveTrainStatus', { connectionId: 'cron-rider' });
  const versionBefore = live.version;
```

This is how a scale-to-zero app avoids paying for upstream polling while idle.
The target owns the wakeup mechanism; the action/mutation behavior stays
portable.

## Test deterministically

`POST /_snapback/api/cron/tick` is an AdminWrite test/operations seam. The
kit's `cronTick()` sends the admin credential, recomputes activation, and
runs due work. Do not wait for wall-clock cadence in acceptance tests.

The acceptance asserts the whole path—tick → action → mutation → live update:

```js source=demos/all-aboard/tests/acceptance/cron.mjs
  await suite.check('scheduler run: action -> mutation -> live delta', async () => {
    const rows = await live.poll();
    assert(live.version > versionBefore, `durable version advanced (${versionBefore} -> ${live.version})`);
    const limited = rows.find((r) => r.patternId === 'sb-limited');
```

`GET /inspect` exposes registered jobs, activation state, next/last timing,
and the bounded recent-run ledger. Assert the job and a successful run so a
vacuous tick cannot pass.

## Run with the scheduler inert

To keep autonomous cron runs out of a test or dev session entirely, start
the server with the scheduler disabled:

```sh
SNAPBACK_CRON_DISABLED=1 snapback   # or: snapback --cron-disabled
```

The switch accepts `1` or `true`; any other value leaves the scheduler on,
so a typo cannot silently disarm production crons. Definitions still load,
validate, and appear in `/inspect` with their ordinary armed/inactive
state — only autonomous claiming stops. `POST /_snapback/api/cron/tick`
keeps working, so a suite drives every tick itself. From an acceptance
suite, pass the kit option instead of hand-building the environment:
`startServer({ ..., cronDisabled: true })` sets `SNAPBACK_CRON_DISABLED=1`
on the child (and refuses to reuse an already-running server, whose
scheduler may be live). See
[LLP 0028 §Scheduler state and run ledger](repo:llp/0028-cron-scheduled-execution.rfc.md).

**The first tick can look early.** `everyMs` schedules anchor their nominal
grid at Unix epoch 0, so an armed job's first evaluation usually finds a
past-due nominal and fires one catch-up run — up to one full interval after
boot, regardless of when your subscription armed it. A 180 s job observed
firing ~180 s after boot "before anything subscribed" is this anchor, not a
bug ([LLP 0028 §Inspection and query
surface](repo:llp/0028-cron-scheduled-execution.rfc.md), ENG-22604). If
that mid-suite run would perturb your assertions, disable the scheduler as
above and tick manually.

Definition generations and run sequences are exact JavaScript-safe integer
identities. The maximum value is usable once; a successor fails before taking
ownership with `SNAPBACK_CRON_DEFINITION_GENERATION_EXHAUSTED` or
`SNAPBACK_CRON_RUN_SEQUENCE_EXHAUSTED`. An out-of-range persisted counter is
`SNAPBACK_CRON_STATE_INVALID`, never an implicit reset. Treat these as terminal
operator diagnostics for that scheduler state rather than retrying the job.
Scheduled-batch staging is atomic: exhaustion in any job publishes none of the
batch's claims. Inspect's consecutive-failure count saturates at the same
portable maximum instead of wrapping.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not schedule a mutation directly.** Cron targets actions; the action
  calls a mutation for durable effects.
- **Do not sleep in tests.** Force an authenticated tick and inspect its run
  ledger; start the suite's server with `cronDisabled: true` so the live
  scheduler cannot commit a competing run mid-assertion.
- **Do not poll while nobody can observe the result.** Use `whileLive` for
  warm-poll products that should scale to zero.
- **Do not disable jitter casually.** Fixed no-jitter schedules need an
  explicit product reason.

# Safe standard data patterns

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

Use `@snapback/codegen/standard-patterns` when a table follows the common
single-owner shape. The helpers generate declarative queries and mutations;
they do not add a second runtime or hide handwritten JavaScript behind the
API.

This surface is partial while its governing soundness RFC is Draft and its
full server-backed cross-user acceptance remains open. The implemented v1
profile is intentionally narrow: owner visibility only, with authorization
and visibility always declared by the caller.

## Declare the owner and continuation boundary

The pagination index is an authorization partition followed by one unique
continuation field. This example uses a server-generated string `pageKey`;
timestamps alone are usually not unique enough for the v1 keyset contract.

```js source=packages/snapback-codegen/standard-patterns.test.mjs
export const todos = defineTable({
  ownerId: v.principal(),
  slug: v.string(),
  title: v.string(),
  pageKey: v.string(),
  createdAt: v.integer(),
  updatedAt: v.integer(),
})
  .index('by_owner_slug', ['ownerId', 'slug'], { unique: true })
  .index('by_owner_page_key', ['ownerId', 'pageKey'], { unique: true })
  .index('by_owner_created', ['ownerId', 'createdAt'])
  .sync();
```

## Generate owner-scoped CRUD

Bind the table into a schema first, then name every generated operation and
declare the owner field. The generated list and get queries include an
executable `ownerId == authUserId()` filter. Create stamps the owner from the
authenticated principal; update and delete re-read the row and guard its owner
inside the transaction.

`createDefaults` and `updateDefaults` use trusted runtime values. `now` becomes
server-derived `runtimeNow()` and `id` becomes server-derived `runtimeId()`;
neither field appears in the public argument schema, so a client cannot forge
it.

```js source=packages/snapback-codegen/standard-patterns.test.mjs
export const { listTodos, getTodo, createTodo, updateTodo, deleteTodo } = defineOwnedCrud({
  table: schema.tables.todos,
  names: {
    list: 'listTodos',
    get: 'getTodo',
    create: 'createTodo',
    update: 'updateTodo',
    delete: 'deleteTodo',
  },
  visibility: { kind: 'owner', field: 'ownerId' },
  createDefaults: { pageKey: 'id', createdAt: 'now', updatedAt: 'now' },
  updateDefaults: { updatedAt: 'now' },
  immutable: ['slug', 'pageKey', 'createdAt'],
  listIndex: 'by_owner_created',
});
```

`listIndex` is required: it names a declared index whose leading field is the
owner field, the generated list orders by that index's field sequence (the
storage layer's implicit `_id` component breaks ties deterministically), and
the helper never emits an unindexed owner scan. `now` defaults bind only to
integer millisecond fields.

Generation fails closed when `visibility` is missing, the owner field is
optional or unsuitable, `listIndex` is absent or not owner-leading, a trusted
default has the wrong field type, the table carries a membership or
permission-backing declaration (generated CRUD refuses authority-bearing
tables), a unique index that excludes the owner field is not named in
`discloseUniqueConflicts` (an undeclared cross-owner conflict would disclose
existence), or an unknown option is present. Cross-owner update and delete
refuse with the same `SNAPBACK_ROW_NOT_FOUND` outcome as a missing row, so
existence is not disclosed at the public boundary.

## Generate a unique lookup

Use a declared unique index that includes the owner field. The helper derives
arguments for the other index fields while retaining the server-derived owner
predicate.

```js source=packages/snapback-codegen/standard-patterns.test.mjs
export const { todoBySlug } = defineOwnedUniqueLookup({
  table: schema.tables.todos,
  name: 'todoBySlug',
  index: 'by_owner_slug',
  visibility: { kind: 'owner', field: 'ownerId' },
});
```

## Generate keyset pages

Keyset pagination emits separate first-page and next-page live queries. Its
index must be unique and contain both the owner and cursor fields; generation
rejects a declaration that would disguise a scan as pagination.

```js source=packages/snapback-codegen/standard-patterns.test.mjs
export const { firstTodoPage, nextTodoPage } = defineOwnedKeysetPages({
  table: schema.tables.todos,
  names: { first: 'firstTodoPage', next: 'nextTodoPage' },
  index: 'by_owner_page_key',
  cursorField: 'pageKey',
  visibility: { kind: 'owner', field: 'ownerId' },
});
```

The default page size is 50. Pass `direction: 'desc'`, a smaller `limit`, or a
different cursor argument name when the declared unique index supports that
shape. The index fields must be exactly `[ownerField, cursorField]`, in that
order. A unique index with a third field is not sufficient because the cursor
may still repeat within one owner's partition. A generated string `pageKey`
using an `id` trusted default is the safe v1 continuation when the natural sort
field, such as a timestamp, is not independently unique.

## Know when to leave the profile

The v1 helpers do not authorize joins, projections, migrations, shared ACLs,
or public rows. Express those semantics directly with the declarative builders
or a JavaScript handler under their governing design. A schema field or index
can prove structure; it cannot prove who may see or mutate a row.

## Anti-patterns

- Do not accept owner, creation time, update time, or generated IDs from client
  arguments when the server can derive them.
- Do not treat `authScopeField` metadata as an authorization predicate; the
  executable owner filter and mutation guard are the enforcement.
- Do not use a non-unique or owner-free index for keyset pagination.
- Do not infer visibility from field names such as `ownerId` or `userId`.
- Do not stretch these helpers over joins, ACLs, or migrations; leave the
  profile and state those semantics explicitly.
