# The authoring loop

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

The cycle you repeat while building on Snapback:

```text
edit snapback/*.mjs  ->  regenerate  ->  run the acceptance suite  ->  inspect
```

From an installed package, start with the same loop through the public CLI:

```sh
snapback doctor --json
snapback new my-app --template todo-contract
cd my-app
bun install
snapback dev snapback
```

`@snapback/cli` supplies the `snapback` command. On Apple-silicon macOS its
optional `@snapback/runtime-darwin-arm64` package carries the prebuilt server
and Hermes framework; `doctor` launches that relocated binary with ambient
dynamic-loader overrides removed. Other host tuples currently report
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_HOST_UNSUPPORTED`—they are not source-build fallbacks disguised
as installs. Public registry publication is still pending. The `@snapback/cli`
npm identity belongs to an unrelated product, so release probes use labeled
`@ccheever/snapback-*` prereleases while keeping the documented source imports
through npm aliases. The retained proof distinguishes immutable-tarball and
public-registry modes and will not treat one as evidence for the other.

## 1. Edit

Change `schema.mjs`, `functions.mjs`, `handlers.mjs`, or `seed.json`
([your first backend](./your-first-backend.md) covers each).

## 2. Regenerate

```sh
node packages/snapback-codegen/index.mjs <app>/snapback
```

Outside this repository, use the packaged equivalent:

```sh
snapback generate snapback
```

`snapback dev snapback` runs that generation first, starts or attaches to the
native server via `.snapback/dev.ready.json`, loads the generated schema and
functions, seeds only a newly created managed database, and watches source
changes through one coalesced generation at a time. The attach path validates
the database target before reading the managed owner-only token. A different
target fails with `SNAPBACK_DEV_SERVER_TARGET_MISMATCH`. If initial attach/load
fails, a server started by this command is stopped. If later generation
succeeds but live load fails, the event state is `generated-but-not-loaded`;
generation errors are the distinct `generation-failed` state.

Codegen is deterministic and **fails closed** — on error it writes nothing
and exits 1 with stable diagnostic codes on stderr, so there is never
silently stale output. On success it prints the `inputsHash` freshness key.
Commit `generated/` with your source change: the server compares hashes and
rejects stale artifacts loudly (`SNAPBACK_STALE_SCHEMA_ARTIFACT_VERSION`,
`SNAPBACK_STALE_CONTRACT_DATA_INPUTS_HASH`) rather than serving them.

If you forget this step, the very first server load or acceptance run tells
you; nothing downstream guesses.

## 3. Run the acceptance suite

Headless first — the required surface is driveable without any UI
(LLP 0012). A suite boots its own isolated server and drives the real
product path:

```sh
node <app>/tests/acceptance/headless.mjs
```

Exit `0` = every declared check passed; `1` = a check failed or the run was
short (zero checks can never pass); `2` = setup error. See
[testing/acceptance](../testing/acceptance.md) for the harness and server
lifecycle discipline.

For a demo in this repo, the whole-repo proof is
`scripts/verify-local-proof` (add `SNAPBACK_VERIFY_EXACT=0` for a
deliberately core-only iteration; merge CI requires the Exact-gated block).

## 4. Inspect

A running server tells you what it is actually serving:

```sh
cargo run                      # prints the admin URL on startup
curl http://127.0.0.1:4287/inspect
```

`GET /inspect` is the public projection (instance, capability facts);
`GET /_snapback/api/inspect` is the admin-gated full view, and the admin
console renders the same surface in a browser — the author's debugger for
"what schema/functions/data does this server hold right now". Structured
failures everywhere carry stable `SNAPBACK_*` diagnostic codes
(`{ code, severity, subsystem, message, details }`), so match on
`error.diagnostic.code`, never on message text.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not hand-edit `generated/` or skip the regenerate step** — the
  server's stale-artifact rejection exists because "it probably still
  matches" was wrong often enough.
- **Do not assert on diagnostic message strings.** Codes are the contract;
  messages are prose.
- **Do not point a new suite at a server you didn't start.** Suites own
  their server lifecycle; see
  [testing/acceptance](../testing/acceptance.md).
- **Do not parse server logs for readiness.** `snapback dev` consumes the
  ready-file descriptor and verifies the live target; log text is not a
  lifecycle protocol.
- **Do not set `SNAPBACK_RUNTIME_BINARY` in ordinary installed projects.** It
  is a contributor/test override. Installed apps should exercise the selected
  platform runtime package so `doctor` verifies the artifact users receive.

# Secrets and deployment config

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

Snapback config is deployment state, separate from app rows. Apps declare
secret entries in source; operators set values through the setup/admin
surface; only actions explicitly naming an entry in `uses` receive a
redacting handle.

## Declare names and acquisition help, never values

`defineConfig` puts public metadata in the generated function manifest:

```js source=demos/all-aboard/snapback/functions.mjs
export const appConfig = defineConfig({
  caltrainFeed: {
    description: '511.org Open Data API key',
    purpose: 'Fetches Caltrain StopMonitoring predictions for live departure boards',
    required: false,
    pool: true,
```

The v1 entry inventory is: `description`, `purpose`, `required`
(default true), `pool`, optional action `probe`, `howToGet`, and
`acquisition` metadata for the setup wizard. V1 values are secret; defaults
and non-secret values are deliberately rejected.

Values never belong in source, manifests, seed data, LLPs, or demo diaries.

## Set and inspect config

Use `/_snapback/admin/setup` for the browser wizard or the admin-gated config
API/host operations for automation. The core operations are `status`,
`set`, `unset`, and `verify`.

`status` reports declaration, set state, member count, source, generation,
and verification—never value bytes:

```js source=demos/all-aboard/tests/acceptance/egress.mjs
  await suite.check('config.status reports names and states, never values', async () => {
    const { status, body, raw } = await configApi(on, 'GET', 'status');
    assertEqual(status, 200, 'status is readable');
    const entry = body.entries.find((e) => e.name === 'feedKeys');
    assert(entry, 'feedKeys is declared');
```

`set` replaces a scalar/pool or appends a pool member; `unset` removes the
deployment value. `verify` invokes the entry's declared action probe and
records only its outcome. Config survives `app.reset` because reset owns app
data, not deployment custody.

## Read through a granted handle

An action names entries in `uses`, then reads `ctx.secrets.get(name)` for the
entry or `ctx.secrets.rotating(name)` for round-robin pool selection. Handle
stringification, interpolation, JSON, and
debug formatting redact. `.expose()` is the narrow, explicit materialization
for building an outbound request; keep the returned string local and
short-lived.

The acceptance proves accidental materialization stays redacted:

```js source=demos/all-aboard/tests/acceptance/egress.mjs
    assertEqual(config.stringified, JSON.stringify(REDACTED), 'JSON.stringify redacts');
    assertEqual(config.template, REDACTED, 'template literal redacts');
    assertEqual(config.concatenated, `prefix:${REDACTED}`, 'string concat redacts');
    assert(!config.stringified.includes('key-'), 'no key material in stringified form');
```

Queries and mutations have no `ctx.secrets`; actions cannot access an entry
outside `uses`. Missing and undeclared entries fail with stable
`SNAPBACK_CONFIG_*` diagnostics.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not put values in `defineConfig`.** It declares names and operator
  help only.
- **Do not pass secrets as function arguments or store them in app tables.**
  Use an action's granted handle.
- **Do not log or return `.expose()`.** Redaction protects the handle, not a
  copied plaintext string.
- **Do not treat `app.reset` as credential rotation.** Use `set`/`unset`
  and verification on the deployment config surface.

# Host operations

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

Host operations give CLIs and agent tools one typed operating surface. The
in-process implementation and `POST /_snapback/api/host-ops` return the same
`hostOpsResult` envelope; operation variants are classified in the route
registry instead of inheriting one overly broad HTTP policy.

## Send one operation, receive one envelope

A request names `operation` plus its typed fields:

```json source=tests/host_ops_v0.rs
        json!({
            "operation": "function.run",
            "function": "createTodo",
            "args": { "title": "from host-ops" },
            "userId": "user_ada",
        }),
```

Every response contains `schemaVersion`, `resultKind: "hostOpsResult"`,
`requestId`, `operation`, `ok`, `target`, optional `authority`,
`artifacts`, `data`, `diagnostics[]`, and `next[]`. A known-but-unbuilt
operation returns `ok: false` with a structured diagnostic, never a fake 404
or empty success.

`artifacts.databaseVersion` contains an integer only when the durable cursor
decodes as an exact portable value. If storage cannot supply a trustworthy
cursor, the envelope becomes `ok: false`, serializes that value as `null`, and
carries the storage diagnostic; tooling must not substitute zero.

## Served request operations

The endpoint serves eight request spellings:

| Request operation | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `app.inspect` | Full runtime/artifact/capability projection. |
| `app.reset` | Coordinated destructive reset, optionally with seed. |
| `schema.load` | Load a generated schema manifest. |
| `functions.load` | Load a generated function/config/cron manifest. |
| `function.run` | Run a query/live query, mutation, or action with its kind-specific gate. |
| `function.explain` | Explain a supported kind; currently `mutationDryRun` is implemented. |
| `auth.mintSession` | Dev/test session mint requiring the process-bound impersonation capability. |
| `auth.rescueCollidingTable` | Operator-only pre-auth catalog collision recovery. |

`host.start`, `host.stop`, and `host.restart` are CLI-only lifecycle
verbs—a running server cannot safely own starting/stopping itself.
`schema.reload`, `functions.reload`, and `acceptance.run` are pinned but
unbuilt and fail as `SNAPBACK_HOST_OP_UNIMPLEMENTED`.

## The exact 13 registry identities

The HTTP request names above expand into these 13 audited operation identities:

1. `host_ops.app.inspect`
2. `host_ops.function.explain`
3. `host_ops.function.explain.impersonated`
4. `host_ops.app.reset`
5. `host_ops.schema.load`
6. `host_ops.functions.load`
7. `host_ops.auth.mintSession`
8. `host_ops.auth.rescueCollidingTable`
9. `host_ops.function.run.query`
10. `host_ops.function.run.mutation`
11. `host_ops.function.run.action`
12. `host_ops.function.run.unknown`
13. `host_ops.function.run.impersonated`

Query/explain reads, durable writes, credential-producing operations, and
dev impersonation therefore keep distinct `RoutePolicy`, authority, effect,
and response-sensitivity classifications even though they share one carrier.

## Respect admin, secret-read, and impersonation gates

The admin credential authenticates the transport; it does not silently invent
an app caller. In sessions mode, sensitive query/explain results additionally
require the bounded admin-secret-read lease. An impersonated branch requires
the process-bound capability and is unavailable in production. Destructive
reset runs through the authorization-stream coordinator and fails closed if
that projection is unavailable.

The partial local `servicePrincipal`/scoped-token slice is admitted only by
generated app-data calls. Host operations—including `function.run`—do not
resolve scoped tokens into authority; use the operation's explicit admin or
dev-impersonation gate instead.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not call internal Rust methods from tooling.** Use the envelope so CLI
  and HTTP behavior stay identical.
- **Do not treat all host ops as AdminWrite.** The registry's kind-specific
  policy is part of the security boundary.
- **Do not interpret an unimplemented diagnostic as an absent operation.**
  Pinned future verbs fail explicitly.
- **Do not place credentials in request ids, logs, or `next[]`.** Credential
  operations use their dedicated response-sensitivity path.

# Diagnostics and local doctoring

Snapback failures carry stable machine identity. Assert and branch on the
`SNAPBACK_*` code; display the message to a human; inspect `details` only
for code-specific facts.

The same contract applies before runtime. Compiler, codegen, dev-server, and
surface-construction failures must carry a stable code, point at the authored
offender (file plus span when known), preserve the first actionable cause, and
report once per source/artifact generation—not once per reactive evaluation.
An authoring failure that can be known during codegen or boot must not be
deferred into an error-shaped data cell.

## Consume the diagnostic shape

The full diagnostic is:

- `code`: stable machine classification;
- `severity`: lowercase `info | warning | error | fatal`;
- `subsystem`: stable owning subsystem;
- `message`: human explanation, not an API;
- `details`: structured code-specific context.

Public unauthenticated projections intentionally drop `message` and
`details`, because they can contain source paths, handler text, arguments, or
operator context. Error envelopes expose the diagnostic at
`error.diagnostic`; some terminal mutation paths also attach a receipt.

## Assert on codes, not prose

The shared acceptance helper demonstrates the rule:

```js source=demos/_kit/harness.mjs
export async function assertThrows(fn, code, message) {
  try {
    await fn();
  } catch (error) {
    const got = error.diagnostic?.code ?? error.message;
    if (code && got !== code) throw new Error(`${message ?? 'wrong error'}: expected ${code}, got ${got}`);
    return error;
  }
  throw new Error(`${message ?? 'expected an error'}: nothing thrown (wanted ${code})`);
}
```

Messages may improve without a compatibility event. A code change is a
contract change and must update its schemas, callers, tests, and docs together.

## Diagnose the vendored Ibex runtime first

Run the read-only doctor before repairing runtime files by hand:

```sh
scripts/ibex-doctor
```

It checks the submodule state, prepared Hermes artifacts/framework, CLI,
runtime-load posture, and required tools. On a clean checkout, bootstrap before
Cargo build/test/run:

```sh
scripts/bootstrap-ibex-runtime
```

The stable bootstrap failure vocabulary is:
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_SOURCE_MISSING`,
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_SUBMODULE_BROKEN`,
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_SUBMODULE_INIT_FAILED`,
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_SUBMODULE_WEDGED`,
`SNAPBACK_CAPABILITY_IBEX_HERMES_MISSING`,
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_HERMES_DOWNLOAD_FAILED`,
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_CARGO_BUILD_FAILED`,
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_RUNTIME_LOAD_FAILED`, and
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_HOST_UNSUPPORTED`.

The doctor additionally distinguishes uninitialized/conflicting/drifted
submodules, a missing vendored CLI, missing Node/Bun/Cargo, and dynamic-loader
configuration. Follow the emitted next checks; do not collapse those states
into “build failed.”

## Preserve the first useful failure

Acceptance harnesses must fail during setup instead of reporting a vacuous
0/0 pass, bound every wait, include the diagnostic body when an assertion
fails, and clean up their server/handles. When one failure cascades, fix and
rerun from the earliest stable code rather than patching later symptoms.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not parse `message` text.** Use `diagnostic.code` and typed details.
- **Do not expose full diagnostics on public endpoints.** Use the public
  classification projection.
- **Do not rebuild Hermes first.** Doctor, then bootstrap from prepared sibling
  artifacts when available.
- **Do not accept a zero-check or timeout-only test result.** Require the
intended diagnostic and non-vacuous witnesses.

Two early data-seam examples are intentionally blocking:

- `FUNCTION_JS_QUERY_STATIC_RESULT_NOT_ROWS` rejects a JavaScript query whose
  handler visibly returns an object literal; return `[row]` or `[]`. Dynamic
  result shapes still meet the runtime rows-array guard.
- `SNAPBACK_CONTRACT_QUERY_UNCONFIGURED` rejects a mounted component's
  `requiredQueries` before the multi-live surface opens any subscription.

# Admin console

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

The admin console is Snapback's browser debugger over
`/_snapback/api/*`. Its Contract app exposes Overview, Schema, Data,
Functions, Secrets, Capabilities, Realtime, and Diagnostics views from the same
inspect/scan/runner/config boundaries used by tests and tools. Its Docs tab
renders the build-matched served guide from the generated manifest; the
console's text renderer never injects guide HTML.

## Launch the built console

Build the static browser and native Exact artifacts, then start Snapback:

```sh
cd admin-ui
./build.sh
cargo run --manifest-path ../Cargo.toml -- --memory
```

The server serves the immutable `dist/` snapshot at
`/_snapback/admin/`. Set `SNAPBACK_ADMIN_DIST` to pin another snapshot; in
a checkout, an unset value discovers `admin-ui/dist` when it exists. If no
dist is available, the route returns a structured missing-dist diagnostic
instead of a second embedded implementation.

Browser baseline:

```sh
cargo run -- --memory
# open the printed admin console URL
```

For a native Exact shell, point `EXACT_APP_CUSTOM_URL` at the
Snapback-served static admin URL. A browser-only dist returns a specific
native-artifact capability diagnostic.

## Use the browser development loop

Run Snapback at a known port, then start the Exact/Contract Vite app:

```sh
cargo run -- --memory --port 4287
SNAPBACK_ADMIN_DEV_API=http://127.0.0.1:4287 bun run --cwd admin-ui dev
```

The dev server regenerates Contract bindings, watches their inputs, and proxies
`/_snapback/api/*` to the configured backend. It binds loopback by default.
Non-loopback proxy exposure requires both
`SNAPBACK_ADMIN_DEV_HOST` and
`SNAPBACK_ADMIN_DEV_ALLOW_NON_LOOPBACK=1`; treat that as exposing a
privileged operator surface.

If the backend is down, the proxy returns
`SNAPBACK_ADMIN_DEV_API_UNREACHABLE` rather than HTML or a blank app.
Static native artifacts remain build-only; request them from the served
`./build.sh` output, not the dev server.

## Authenticate the operator surface

Loopback reads are open until an admin token exists; writes and non-loopback
access follow the server's admin policy. Use the printed/token-file credential,
never app session credentials. Sessions-mode sensitive reads use a separate
short-lived admin-secret-read lease; neither credential substitutes for the
other.

The UI clears submitted credentials and renders hostile diagnostics as text:

```js source=admin-ui/tests/fatal-rendering.mjs
assert.equal(root.children[0].tagName, 'pre');
assert.equal(
  root.children[0].textContent,
  `Admin console failed to start:\n${hostile}`,
);
assert.equal('innerHTML' in root.children[0], false);
```

The production browser proof also enforces CSP hashes, Trusted Types, zero
runtime exceptions, zero console errors, and zero policy violations.

## Debug through declared views

- **Overview/Capabilities/Realtime/Diagnostics:** inspect target, artifacts,
  capability gaps, delivery state, receipts, and stable codes.
- **Schema/Data:** inspect declared tables and page through rows; private reads
  remain subject to secret-read scope/budgets.
- **Functions:** run queries, mutations, and actions through the classified
  direct-runner boundary and inspect captured reads/writes.
- **Secrets:** see declaration/set/verification state and run declared probes;
  values never render.
- **Docs:** navigate the same manifest/corpus served at `/_snapback/guide`,
  with response hash/build identity checked before a page renders.

Use the [host operations](./host-ops.md) page for automation and
[diagnostics](./diagnostics.md) for code-driven troubleshooting.

## Verify the Contract/Exact seam

The build preset owns plugin ordering, route/entry preflight, static/native
targets, and the admin base-path rewrite. Snapback's Exact discovery/conformance
helpers remain optional for ordinary core work:

```sh
node packages/snapback-contract/exact-conformance.mjs
node packages/snapback-contract/exact-conformance.mjs --require
node packages/snapback-contract/exact-conformance.mjs --run
```

`--require` makes a lane fail unless Exact registers the provider suite;
`--run` invokes Exact's registered check. Generated descriptor/project
semantics are covered by the Contract adapter acceptance, not by a hand-written
admin binding layer.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not run the privileged dev proxy on a LAN accidentally.**
- **Do not point a native shell at a browser Vite surface.** Use the built
  Snapback-served admin URL.
- **Do not persist admin or secret-read credentials in UI state/storage.**
- **Do not bypass generated Contract bindings with a second admin UI.**

# Live queries

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

A live query is an ordinary query definition that clients can subscribe
to: subscribers get an authoritative initial snapshot **with** the
subscription (never a prime race), then server-pushed updates over the
durable lane as commits change the result.

## Define one

Mark the definition live — declarative or JS style
([your first backend](../getting-started/your-first-backend.md) covers the
two styles):

```js source=demos/todo/snapback/functions.mjs
export const listTodos = defineJsLiveQuery({
  args: {},
  source: 'handlers.mjs',
  exportName: 'listTodos',
  reads: ['todos'],
  authScopeField: 'userId',
```

`defineLiveQuery` is the declarative twin (same spec as `defineQuery` plus
`defaultLive: false` to make live opt-in per subscription). `reads:` and
`authScopeField:` matter: they drive invalidation and per-principal scoping
(see [auth](../auth/sessions-and-principals.md)). Subscribing to a non-live
function fails with `SNAPBACK_FUNCTION_NOT_LIVE`.

## Subscribe

`client.liveQuery(ref, options)` returns a handle with the snapshot already
applied — `rows`, `connection`, `poll()`, `dispose()`:

```js source=demos/todo/tests/acceptance/headless.mjs
    const handle = await db.liveQuery(api.listTodos, { connectionId: 'client_a', userId: ADA });
    assertEqual(handle.rows.length, 3, 'snapshot rows');
```

Cross-client delivery is the point — one client mutates, the other's
subscription updates:

```js source=demos/todo/tests/acceptance/headless.mjs
    const b = await db.liveQuery(api.listTodos, { connectionId: 'client_b', userId: ADA });
    assertEqual(b.rows.length, 3, 'b initial');
    await db.mutate(api.createTodo, { args: { title: 'Added by another client' }, userId: ADA });
    const rows = await b.poll();
    assertEqual(rows.length, 4, 'b did not receive realtime update');
```

Key options: `transport: 'stream'` for durable WebSocket push (`'poll'` is
the default, cadence `pollCadenceMs`, with `fallbackToPoll` when a stream
can't be established), `onUpdate(rows, meta)`, `onConnectionChange`,
`connectionId` (one shared socket per connection id multiplexes all of that
connection's live handles), and per-socket `stream:` tuning
(heartbeat/freshness/reconnect). Always `dispose()` handles you created.
The supplied `connectionId` is a readable client-local label; the kit resolves
and refreshes its opaque granted wire id for high-level calls. A low-level
adapter constructing raw frames must use
`(await client.connectionGrant(label)).id`, never the readable label.

## Logical keyed bindings

One physical handle is not necessarily one component binding. The dynamic
Contract provider lets Exact key a logical attempt by opaque authority
partition, stable descriptor identity and compatibility token, and canonical
arguments. Same-key siblings share data/error/reconnect state but dispose by
independent refcount; different args, descriptors, providers, or authority
partitions stay isolated. An authority change clears predecessor rows before
reopening, so a late result cannot cross the privacy cut.

This layer is for generated/framework integrations. Direct headless callers
still own each `client.liveQuery()` handle they create. See
[the Contract adapter](../clients/contract-adapter.md) for the shipped dynamic
mode and its current live-push/no-offline profile boundary.

## What arrives: replace and delta

Durable updates carry a `meta.kind`: `live_replace` (a full snapshot of the
result) or `live_delta` (incremental add/remove — the analyzable
unordered/filtered subset gets deltas; ordered queries fall back to
replace; LLP 0008 §DK-3). `resync_required` tells the client to
re-snapshot; `authorization_invalidation` is the auth barrier
([protecting data](../auth/protecting-data.md)). A subscription
asserts on delta kinds like this:

```js source=demos/_kit/tests/live-delta-e2e.mjs
  const handle = await db.liveQuery('listMine', {
    connectionId: 'delta_conn',
    userId: ADA,
    transport: 'stream',
    stream: { heartbeatIntervalMs: 200, freshnessBudgetMs: 800, reconnectBaseDelayMs: 100, reconnectMaxDelayMs: 400 },
    onUpdate: rec.onUpdate,
  });
```

Membership-gated live replacement does not make a query safe for offline
retention. V1 refuses retained role-gated queries until an authorized lease can
bind the exact membership declaration/resource dependency and expiry floor.

## Connection state an author can observe

The stream manager emits `'connecting'`, `'open'`, `'lost'`
(`{ wasOpen }`), `'budget-missed'` (socket claims open but the freshness
budget lapsed), and `'closed'`. The kit derives a per-query `connection`
axis from these and pushes it through `onConnectionChange`; the conventional
author-facing mapping (from the cursors-web hook) is:

```ts source=demos/cursors-web/surfaces/react/src/useCursorRoom.ts
export type ConnectionAxis = 'connecting' | 'live' | 'stale' | 'disconnected';
```

`open → live`; `budget-missed`/`lost → stale` (degraded — render retained
data, marked); `closed → disconnected`. Defaults:
`LIVE_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_MS = 5_000`, `LIVE_FRESHNESS_BUDGET_MS = 15_000`,
reconnect backoff 250ms → 10s. The
[headless client](../clients/headless.md) owns this state machine; the
[Contract adapter](../clients/contract-adapter.md) and React arm consume it.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not poll a query you can subscribe to.** `liveQuery` exists;
  hand-rolled `setInterval` re-query loops re-derive a worse version of the
  poll transport and never get durable push.
- **Do not treat a socket as fresh because it is open.** `budget-missed`
  exists precisely because "open" and "fresh" diverge; consume the
  connection axis, not `isOpen()`.
- **Do not leak handles.** Every `liveQuery`/overlay handle is `dispose()`d
  in teardown (React: effect cleanup; suites: `cleanups`).

# Ephemeral realtime state

> **Local target only.** This page describes the process-local dev/test
> target. A hosted target needs sticky room routing or a shared room adapter;
> Snapback does not currently claim that hosted capability.

Ephemeral collections are typed, authorized, TTL-bounded latest-state maps for
presence, cursors, selections, typing, drag state, and live viewport state.
They are deliberately lossy: if a value must survive restart, support offline
reads, or enter history/audit, put it in a durable table instead.

Start with the [presence-cursors recipe](../recipes/presence-cursors.md) when
building a feature. Use this page when choosing collection options or handling
recovery.

## Declare the complete collection contract

One collection declaration contains every routing, ownership, budget,
delivery, validation, and access fact:

```js source=demos/cursors-web/snapback/schema.mjs
    webCursors: ephemeral.collection({
      scope: { roomId: v.string() },
      routing: ['roomId'],
      key: 'connection',
      ttlMs: 5_000,
      maxTtlMs: 30_000,
      maxValueBytes: 1_024,
      publishRate: { sustainedHz: 20, burst: 40 },
      delivery: { mode: 'latest', dispatchMs: 33 },
      value: v.object({
        x: v.number(),
        y: v.number(),
        name: v.string(),
        color: v.string(),
        updatedAt: v.optional(v.number()),
      }),
      publish: allow.all(),
      subscribe: allow.all(),
    }),
```

The option inventory is:

| Option | Local contract |
| --- | --- |
| `scope` | Required non-empty validator object. Its normalized values partition snapshots, fan-out, and authorization. |
| `routing` | Defaults to every scope field; must be a non-empty, duplicate-free subset of `scope`. |
| `key` | `connection` by default; also `session`, `user`, or `custom`. |
| `ttlMs` | Required positive default lease. There is no immortal entry. |
| `maxTtlMs` | Defaults to and may not exceed 30,000ms; must be at least `ttlMs`. |
| `maxValueBytes` / `hardMaxValueBytes` | Defaults 1,024/4,096 bytes; neither may cross the 4 KiB local hard cap. |
| `publishRate` | Defaults to `{ sustainedHz: 20, burst: 60 }`, enforced per connection/collection. |
| `delivery` | Defaults to `{ mode: 'latest', dispatchMs: 33 }`; `latest` is the only shipped mode. |
| `publish` / `subscribe` | Both required explicit policies: `allow.all()` or `allow.roomPermission(prefix)`. |
| `value` | Required portable validator; generated clients and the server validate it. |
| `targets` | Defaults to `local-dev-sqlite-ibex`; codegen rejects an undeclared selected target. |
| `maxPendingEphemeralKeys` | Defaults to 1,024, bounding coalesced keys retained for dispatch. |

Codegen rejects unsafe routing, absent TTL/auth, unsupported modes/targets,
invalid validators, and over-budget declarations before it writes artifacts.
Do not treat authoring defaults as hosted scale promises.

## Choose a key mode deliberately

- `connection` gives each active connection its own value and reclaims it on
  disconnect or expiry. Its key is the opaque id granted to the transport,
  not the app's readable connection label. It is the normal cursor/presence
  choice.
- `session` derives the key from the authenticated session, so reconnecting
  can refresh the same lease. A caller-supplied session id is only an
  assertion and must match transport authority.
- `user` derives the key from the authenticated user. Multiple connections
  refresh one shared lease; use it only when presence privacy permits.
- `custom` accepts several connection-owned keys. Until generated
  key-specific authorization exists, only the creating connection may replace
  or delete each key.

Never put a display name or caller-asserted user id in charge of ownership.
The transport-derived connection/session/user identity is authoritative.

## Authorize publish and subscribe separately

`allow.all()` is explicit public room access. For protected rooms, use the
same room permission prefix on publish and subscribe and grant the normalized
permission through the connection authority:

```js fragment reason="Policy fragment; protected room fixture uses a different domain-specific prefix."
publish: allow.roomPermission('boardPresence'),
subscribe: allow.roomPermission('boardPresence'),
```

The matching permission string is
`SnapbackClient.roomPermission('boardPresence', scope)`. A room protected by
durable membership also participates in the authorization-invalidation
barrier. Membership-backed room authority binds to the declaration's stable id,
not a table name or ambient role string; removing or downgrading a required role
quiesces affected room sinks before the commit becomes visible. Custom-key
authorization beyond connection ownership is not shipped.

## Subscribe to snapshot plus deltas

`subscribeEphemeral(ref, { connectionId, scope, ... })` registers the lane
consumer before requesting its authoritative snapshot, buffers in-flight
deltas, then applies them after the snapshot boundary. The returned overlay
provides `currentEntries()`, `onChange`, `publish`, `delete`, `drain`, and
`dispose`, plus `grantedConnectionId`: the exact opaque connection id used by
that successful subscribe. Compare a connection-owned entry's `key` with this
field to identify self. Do not compare it with the readable `connectionId`
argument, which only keys the client's grant/socket registries and may diverge
after collision or mint-only containment.

Each current entry is:

```text fragment reason="Normalized public entry shape assembled by EphemeralOverlay.currentEntries()."
{ key, value, expiresAtMs, receivedAtMs, scopeEpoch, entryVersion }
```

The client prunes by the server-stamped expiry deadline. Server expiry,
explicit delete, and disconnect normally emit remove deltas, but TTL is the
backstop when that remove is lost.

## Treat epochs and versions as one-room coordinates

`entryVersion` is a monotonic room-local high-water coordinate, meaningful
only for one collection/scope and within one `scopeEpoch`. The overlay ignores
stale versions and keeps bounded tombstones so an old upsert cannot resurrect
a removed entry.

An epoch mismatch, queue overflow, or connection-wide continuity loss produces
the level-triggered `needs_resync` state. Blank/degrade the UI, create a fresh
overlay with `subscribeEphemeral`, attach its listener, then dispose the old
overlay. Do not compare ephemeral versions with durable commit versions, and
do not reopen a connection-poisoned overlay with a delayed snapshot.

## Use generated Contract links

Codegen emits a typed `*.ephemeral.ts` read descriptor, a
`*.publish.ts` descriptor, their Contract metadata, and runtime links. A
Contract component reads the map as an `ephemeral` binding:

```contract source=demos/cursors-web/surfaces/contract/app.contract
  ephemeral cursors = webCursors({ roomId: "lobby" })
```

The surface prewarms the room and configures the generated links; authored
`publish ... rate=N` channels are statically checked against the generated
publish budget. Keep imperative overlays in headless/React code and generated
ephemeral links in Contract code—do not mix a second polling or publish lane
into the same surface.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not store transient motion in tables.** Durable commits and history are
  the wrong correctness model for cursor samples.
- **Do not invent global/unscoped rooms.** Scope is the fan-out and
  authorization boundary.
- **Do not retry rate-limit failures blindly.** Lower the publisher rate and
  observe rejections.
- **Do not trust deltas after `needs_resync`.** Establish a fresh snapshot
  boundary.
- **Do not claim multi-instance presence.** The current shipped adapter is
  process-local.
- **Do not derive self from a readable connection label.** The granted id on
  the overlay is the connection-owned lease key.

---

# Recipe: presence cursors

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

"Two users see each other's cursors" is ephemeral state, not app data: it
lives in typed in-memory rooms with TTL expiry and connection-owned
cleanup (LLP 0013) — never in tables, never polled. The working reference
is `demos/cursors-web`. This recipe is the shortest paved implementation;
the [ephemeral-state reference](../realtime/ephemeral-state.md) inventories
every collection option, key mode, recovery rule, and Contract link.

## 1. Declare the ephemeral collection in the schema

An ephemeral collection is declared beside your tables, with its scope
(the room key), keying, TTL, payload budget, and publish rate all typed
and enforced server-side. The shape (this one is todo-v2's presence
collection; cursors-web's `webCursors` follows the same form):

```js source=demos/todo-v2/snapback/schema.mjs
  ephemeral: defineEphemeral({
    todoPresence: ephemeral.collection({
      scope: { listId: v.string() },
      routing: ['listId'],
      key: 'connection',
      ttlMs: 20_000,
      maxTtlMs: 30_000,
      maxValueBytes: 512,
      publishRate: { sustainedHz: 20, burst: 40 },
      delivery: { mode: 'latest', dispatchMs: 33 },
      value: v.object({
        name: v.string(),
        editing: v.optional(v.boolean()),
      }),
      publish: allow.all(),
      subscribe: allow.all(),
```

`key: 'connection'` makes the lease key the publisher's opaque,
server-granted connection id—presence provenance without a spoofable app
field. The readable `connectionId` that app code passes to the kit is only a
local grant/socket label; it may match the lease key after initial dev
adoption, but collision or mint-only containment makes them diverge.
Regenerate after editing (the generated publish descriptor carries the
budget facts your client code should assert against, e.g. cursors-web
checks its declared publish rate fits `sustainedHz` at init).

## 2. Subscribe to the room

`subscribeEphemeral` returns an overlay that applies the authoritative
snapshot, then buffers and applies deltas from the shared live socket
(registered before the snapshot request, so nothing can fall in the gap):

```ts source=demos/cursors-web/surfaces/react/src/useCursorRoom.ts
    void client
      .subscribeEphemeral(cursorsRef, { connectionId, scope: { roomId } })
      .then((overlay) => {
        if (disposed) {
          // StrictMode double-mount: the first effect's subscribe may resolve
          // after its cleanup ran — never leak that overlay's lane consumer.
          overlay.dispose();
          return;
        }
        overlayRef.current = overlay;
        subscribedRef.current = true;
        offChange = overlay.onChange(handleChange);
        recompute();
      })
```

Read entries with `overlay.currentEntries()` — each is
`{ key, value, expiresAtMs, ... }`; `entry.key ===
overlay.grantedConnectionId` is "self". `grantedConnectionId` is captured
from the exact successful subscribe attempt, including a token-refresh retry.
`onChange` also delivers a level-triggered `'needs_resync'` when
connection continuity is lost (epoch boundary / queue overflow): present
degraded state, then re-enter with a fresh `subscribeEphemeral` and swap
the overlay.

## 3. Publish samples under the declared budget

```ts source=demos/cursors-web/surfaces/react/src/useCursorRoom.ts
      overlay
        .publish(value, { ttlMs: PRESENCE_TTL_MS })
        .then(() => {
          state.published += 1;
          if (state.establishedAtMs === null) state.establishedAtMs = Date.now();
        })
        .catch(() => {
          state.rejected += 1;
        });
```

The server enforces the schema's rate and payload budgets — count
rejections rather than retrying blindly. Entries expire on the
server-stamped `expiresAtMs`; the reference hook freezes TTL-pruning while
the connection is `stale`/`disconnected` so departed cursors stay
renderable during degradation instead of silently vanishing.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not store presence in tables.** Cursor positions in app data means
  commits, versions, and history for state that is worthless in ten
  seconds; the ephemeral store exists for exactly this.
- **Do not invent your own presence keys.** `key: 'connection'` gives you
  provenance; a custom name field is spoofable and duplicates on refresh.
- **Do not compare entry keys with the readable connection label.** Compare
  with `overlay.grantedConnectionId`; only the server grant is lease identity.
- **Do not publish above the declared budget** — assert your sample rate
  fits the generated budget facts at init, like the reference hook does.

# Recipe: hidden hands

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

Per-principal secrecy over shared data: a card game where every player
queries the same `myHand` function and sees only their own cards — live,
across logout, and honestly offline. The working reference is
`demos/card-game`, and every claim here is asserted by its acceptance
suite (which runs in the local proof).

Prerequisite: sessions-mode auth —
[sessions and principals](../auth/sessions-and-principals.md). For the complete
grant/invalidation/lease contract behind this recipe, use
[protecting data](../auth/protecting-data.md).

## One query, disjoint worlds

Each player signs in (email code → session) and calls the same query with
no owner argument. The query's explicit
`eq('ownerId', authUserId())` predicate compares rows with the
server-derived session principal:

```js source=demos/card-game/snapback/functions.mjs
  filter: [
    eq('ownerId', authUserId()),
    eq('gameId', arg('gameId')),
  ],
```

For JS live queries, `authScopeField` can additionally declare the principal
field to the live matcher; it never substitutes for the ownership predicate.

```js source=demos/card-game/tests/acceptance/authority-scope.mjs
  const [adaResult, graceResult] = await Promise.all([
    ada.client.query('myHand', { args: { gameId } }),
    grace.client.query('myHand', { args: { gameId } }),
  ]);
```

The suite then asserts the two result sets are disjoint — no card leaks
across principals, finite or live.

## Logout blanks yours, only yours

```js source=demos/card-game/tests/acceptance/authority-scope.mjs
  await ada.client.authLogout();
  assert.deepEqual(adaSurface.boundary.current('hand'), []);
  assert.deepEqual(
    graceSurface.boundary.current('hand').map(({ card }) => card),
    ['king-clubs', 'ten-diamonds'],
  );
```

The invalidation barrier is per-principal and immediate on live
boundaries (LLP 0053).

## Offline retention ends at the lease deadline, exactly

With a client store, an authorized retained query survives a cold process
start while the server is down — readable, marked `stale` — until the
signed lease's client deadline, after which store validation deletes the
hidden rows before any fallback could serve them:

```js source=demos/card-game/tests/acceptance/authority-scope.mjs
  const offlineSurface = await trackSurface(coldGraceOptions);
  assert.equal(offlineSurface.retained(), true);
  assert.equal(offlineSurface.connection(), 'stale');
```

```js source=demos/card-game/tests/acceptance/authority-scope.mjs
  const expiredState = await coldGraceStore.snapshot();
  assert.equal(expiredState.retained[retainedQueryKey], undefined);
  assert.equal(expiredState.queryAuthorization[retainedQueryKey]?.lease, null);
```

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not filter secrets client-side.** Sending the whole game state and
  hiding other hands in the UI is not secrecy; the scoping must be the
  server's.
- **Do not cache authorized rows outside the client store.** The store is
  what enforces the lease deadline; a side cache outlives authorization.
- **Do not pass the player as a query argument.** The server derives the
  principal; an owner argument is spoofable and is rejected in sessions
  mode.

# Offline retention and mutation replay

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

The Contract adapter can retain the last authoritative query snapshot, render
derived optimistic changes while offline, and replay a durable mutation outbox
in order after reconnect. It reports this as `Parity` only when every
required proof is present; otherwise the surface stays honestly `Online`.

## Enable the complete client-store contract

Pass a durable `clientStore` (localStorage on web; memory only for tests) and
a complete retained identity: app id, database id, target-profile id, and
version-stream id. The generated Contract data manifest must claim
`offlineReplay`, and every mutation exposed by the surface must have a
derivable declarative plan.

If any identity or replay proof is missing, queued writes and retention are
disabled instead of being rebound to a guessed backend. A changed artifact or
authority scope quarantines/deletes the old privacy-bearing state before the
new scope can inspect it.

For `AgentAuthorityFence`, the durable authority key is a canonical SHA-256
identity over the actor, credential id and generation, and grant id. Token id,
bearer bytes, and carrier generation are deliberately excluded: rotating a
token for that same tuple can replay its existing queue, while changing any
durable tuple coordinate advances the authority epoch and deletes predecessor
work. Every replay still resolves and validates a current scoped token before
the server acts. Agent authority does not enable retained service-principal
reads in v1.

Production CLI and daemon replay requires both a durable Contract
`clientStore` and a filesystem-backed `AgentAuthorityFence`; the in-memory
custody adapter is test-only. Construct the Contract surface before manually
synchronizing the fence. Surface construction registers the physical store as
a barrier participant before it performs the strict server handshake, so a
restart that finds an interrupted `clearing` transition replays that store's
epoch-bound deletion before custody can settle. Reversing that order can leave
predecessor queue data outside the recovered authority barrier and is refused
by the supported construction path.

The surface re-synchronizes durable custody before client-store reads,
retained publication, enqueue/acknowledgement, and final replay dispatch. A
missed process-local or BroadcastChannel wakeup therefore cannot expose or
settle predecessor rows and queued writes under a peer successor. The visible
surface blanks at the authority cut; durable predecessor work remains owned by
the barrier until its exact deletion/transition settles rather than being
silently acknowledged or discarded.

Terminal replay is explicit, not inferred from a null browser principal scope
(Agent successors also have no browser principal scope). An exact-current
nonterminal Agent successor preserves its already-committed store bytes. An
exact-current terminal replay verifies or reapplies deletion. If terminal B
finds that shared primary custody now belongs to A, Snapback leaves A's primary
row and any A-keyed local store untouched, but purges and unbinds a local store
still keyed to B so stale retained/queued B data cannot survive behind the
terminal witness.

Client-store write generations do not wrap. The maximum safe integer is
reserved for the terminal privacy cut; an already-exhausted bound store exposes
no retained or queued data even if durable replacement fails. A clean marker at
that final identity can be replayed without another write, but requires explicit
store replacement before any successor bind.

## Boot from retained rows honestly

An online boot publishes and stores the authoritative snapshot. If a later
boot cannot reach the same backend, the adapter may publish those retained
rows with `retained() === true` and connection `'stale'`:

```js source=packages/snapback-contract/offline-replay.test.mjs
// New store + new adapter instance models an app reload. The live request
// fails, retained rows boot stale, and the durable create overlay re-applies.
const secondStore = createMemorySnapbackClientStore({ state: sharedState });
const second = await makeSurface(secondStore);
assert.equal(second.retained(), true);
assert.equal(second.connection(), 'stale');
assert.equal(second.boundary.current('todos')[0]._id, todoId);
```

A first run with no retained snapshot fails with the original network error.
Retained data is never relabeled `live`.

For sessions-mode private rows, ordinary retention is insufficient. The server
must issue an authorized lease and the store must delete rows exactly at its
deadline. That stricter subset is taught in
[hidden hands](../recipes/hidden-hands.md).

## Queue one deterministic mutation identity

Before an offline optimistic change becomes visible, the store durably
allocates:

- an opaque `clientMutationId`;
- a monotonic local sequence (ordering never comes from wall-clock time);
- the function and canonical arguments;
- the authority/artifact scope;
- one deterministic `ctxLedger` containing generated time/id answers.

The derived optimistic overlay consumes the **same** ledger, so a replayed
insert uses the id the UI already rendered. If durable enqueue fails, the
optimistic change is rolled back before any server contact.

The test queues create → toggle → delete and proves durable ordering:

```js source=packages/snapback-contract/offline-replay.test.mjs
const queued = await secondStore.pendingMutations();
assert.deepEqual(queued.map((entry) => entry.function), [
  'createTodo',
  'setCompleted',
  'deleteTodo',
]);
assert.deepEqual(queued.map((entry) => entry.sequence), [1, 2, 3]);
```

## Replay and settle without guessing

Reconnect delivers records in sequence with the original mutation id, ledger,
and authority descriptor. The server settles that id atomically with the data
commit. If a response is lost after commit, redelivery returns the stored
result rather than applying the mutation twice:

```js source=packages/snapback-contract/offline-replay.test.mjs
const replay = await second.reconnect();
assert.deepEqual(replay, { replayed: 3, failed: 0 });
assert.deepEqual(client.state.applied, ['createTodo', 'setCompleted', 'deleteTodo']);
assert.deepEqual(client.state.rows, []);
assert.equal(second.pendingCount(), 0);
```

The client retains a successful/rejected settlement until the server proves it
received the acknowledgement. A Snapback-origin terminal receipt proves the
origin saw the request and any piggyback acknowledgements. A receipt-less
proxy/network failure proves neither, so both records remain durable for the
next reconnect.

## Derive, then reconcile optimistic rows

Declarative mutation plans produce the local overlay; avoid a second handwritten
reducer. Server rows remain authoritative:

- success reconciles the optimistic wave with the committed result;
- a structured rejection removes/rebases the prediction and exposes the
  diagnostic;
- a connectivity ambiguity keeps the durable record and marks the surface
  stale;
- an artifact or authority change clears/quarantines old rows and writes before
  publishing the successor scope.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not call a surface Parity because it has localStorage.** The manifest,
  identities, derivable plans, store, and authority fences must all agree.
- **Do not generate a fresh id or timestamp on replay.** Reuse the captured
  mutation id and deterministic ledger.
- **Do not drop a queued write on a receipt-less 502.** The origin outcome is
  ambiguous.
- **Do not serve retained rows as live.** Render the stale connection axis.
- **Do not cache authorized rows outside the lease-aware store.** Use the
  authorized-retention path or keep the surface online-only.
- **Do not key an agent outbox by token id.** Tokens are live carriers; the
  server-issued descriptor and durable grant tuple own replay identity.

# Acceptance testing

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

Snapback apps are proven **headless-first** (LLP 0012): the required
surface is a suite that boots a real server, loads the real generated
artifacts, and drives the product client — no UI in the loop. UI arms
(Contract, React) are additional surfaces over the same backend.

## The harness

`demos/_kit/harness.mjs` provides a dependency-free suite with structured,
machine-readable results and **vacuous-pass protection** — a run that
executes zero non-skipped checks (or fewer checks than it declared) can never
report success. Explicit remote-dependency skips remain visible evidence, but
they are never counted as passes:

```js source=demos/_kit/harness.mjs
    finish() {
      const passed = results.filter((r) => r.ok).length;
      const skipped = results.filter((r) => r.outcome === 'skip').length;
      const failed = results.length - passed - skipped;
      const total = results.length;
      // ENG-22486: zero checks (or a short run against a declared count) can
      // never be a pass — a pre-check throw that skips the checks must fail.
      let shortfall = null;
      if (total === 0 || passed + failed === 0) {
        shortfall = 'zero checks ran';
      } else if (expectedChecks !== null && total !== expectedChecks) {
        shortfall = `ran ${total}/${expectedChecks} expected checks`;
      }
      const ok = failed === 0 && shortfall === null;
      const report = { title, passed, skipped, failed, total, ok, results };
```

Use `createSuite(title, { expectedChecks })` and `await suite.check(name,
fn)` per behavior; `runAcceptance(suite, body, { cleanups })` is the shared
runner tail — it surfaces setup errors with their stacks, prints a
machine-readable JSON report line after running every cleanup in reverse
order, and exits `0` (pass), `1` (check failure or short run), or `2`
(setup/teardown infrastructure error). Cleanup rejections cannot turn a
passing check run green: the final report has `ok: false` and retains every
failure in `cleanupErrors`, including stable error codes and process-tree
attestation details when supplied by the lifecycle helper. `suite.skip(...)`
is reserved for an explicitly classified unavailable remote dependency; it
adds a structured skipped result, cannot satisfy a required all-skipped run,
and is never represented as a passing check.
Assertion helpers: `assert`, `assertEqual`, and
`assertThrows(fn, code, msg)`, which matches `error.diagnostic.code` —
stable codes, never message text. `requireBunRuntime(label)` guards suites
that must run under bun.

## Server lifecycle: isolated, provenance-verified, owned

`startServer` from `demos/_kit/server-process.mjs` is the only way a suite
should obtain a server:

```js source=demos/todo/tests/acceptance/headless.mjs
const server = await startServer({ port: 4399, db: ':memory:', cwd: repoRoot,
  provenance: { appId: 'todo', artifactsPath: join(repoRoot, 'demos', 'todo', 'snapback', 'generated', 'artifacts.json') } });
const db = new SnapbackClient(server.baseUrl, server.clientOptions);
```

What it guarantees:

- **Isolated ports by default.** Ordinary starts pass `--port 0`, so the OS
  assigns a port and the child reports its actual bound URL through a ready
  file; always use the returned `server.baseUrl`, never the port you asked
  for.
- **Reuse only with verified provenance.** A server already listening is
  reused only when its loaded bundle identity matches the declared
  `provenance` (or `binaryProvenance`); any mismatch — or no declared
  identity — refuses reuse and spawns a fresh isolated server instead.
- **Owned teardown.** The returned handle's `.stop()` tears down the whole
  process tree the harness itself started (SIGTERM then SIGKILL, attested
  group exit). Nothing else is ever killed.
- `--memory` for `db: ':memory:'`; file-backed servers take an exclusive
  sidecar lock so two servers can't mutate one database.

### Keep cron out of your suite

If the app declares cron jobs, a live scheduler can commit runs mid-suite —
and the first one can land surprisingly early: an `everyMs` job's nominal
grid anchors at Unix epoch 0, so its first tick can fire up to one full
interval after boot **regardless of when demand arrived** ([LLP 0028
§Inspection and query
surface](repo:llp/0028-cron-scheduled-execution.rfc.md), ENG-22604). Start
the server with the scheduler inert and drive ticks yourself:

```js fragment reason="illustrative option on the startServer call above"
const server = await startServer({ db: ':memory:', cwd: repoRoot, cronDisabled: true });
```

`cronDisabled: true` sets `SNAPBACK_CRON_DISABLED=1` on the child (the CLI
form is `--cron-disabled`) and refuses to reuse an already-running server,
whose scheduler may be live. Definitions still load and inspect; the
admin `cronTick()` seam keeps working, so scheduled behavior stays testable
deterministically — see [backend/cron](../backend/cron.md).

If a suite hand-spawns `snapback`/`cargo run` without a controlling terminal,
it must pass a fresh `--ready-file <path>`. The process-bound impersonation
capability is published only to that owner-only sidecar; it is never written to
captured stdout/stderr. Prefer `startServer`, which already owns this handshake.

Then load and drive the app exactly as production clients do — see
[your first backend](../getting-started/your-first-backend.md) for
`loadSchema`/`loadFunctions`/`reset`/`seed` and the query/mutation calls,
and [realtime/live-queries](../realtime/live-queries.md) for asserting on
live updates.

## What a good suite asserts

The todo headless suite (`demos/todo/tests/acceptance/headless.mjs`) is the
model: authoritative reads after writes, structured mutation results
(`result`, `changed_count`), server-owned system fields, live snapshot +
cross-client realtime delivery, error paths by diagnostic code, and
admin-gated operations with the server-issued `server.adminToken`.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not claim a fixed port and kill whatever holds it.** Request an
  OS-assigned port (the default); reuse a server only after provenance
  verification; stop only processes your own harness started.
  `server-process.mjs` implements exactly this discipline — inherit it.
- **Do not swallow setup errors into a green run.** Zero-check and
  short-run passes are structurally impossible under the harness; keep
  `expectedChecks` declared so they stay impossible.
- **Do not detach or catch-and-ignore cleanup promises.** Return each cleanup
  promise through the shared `cleanups` stack. The runner attempts all of them
  in reverse order and fails the run if any cleanup rejects.
- **Do not assert on diagnostic message text.** Use `assertThrows(fn,
  'SNAPBACK_...')` against the code.
